  • In a recent development, the study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life.
  • Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a upcoming October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

In a recent development, the study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis people weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She indicates more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Industry observers note that deep sleep is one of the most key stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu indicates it’s vital for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

Sources indicate that if you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

Sources indicate that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

Recent findings suggest that the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

Industry observers note that yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

This is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

According to recent reports, this recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a latest bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” notes Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any new or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”.

Recent findings suggest that your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” states Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

In a recent development, when hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”.

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” claims Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

Sources indicate that if you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any upcoming, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” indicates Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”.

Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

You’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. True to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

In a recent development, I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

In a recent development, in a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

In a recent development, this is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

In a recent development, would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table rapidly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

When it comes to versatile sides, it’s difficult to beat classic roasted potatoes. They complete practically any main they’re served alongside! In this recipe, the humble potato is transformed into perfectly crispy, herby bites that put any frozen bag to shame.

If you’re not into creamy, melty macaroni and cheese with an insanely satisfying cheese-pull, then you might want to find another mac recipe. Sorry, but this slow-cooker macaroni and cheese is just too darn dreamy.

Would Grandma really be all that upset if you tried a new stuffing this holiday? Her cornbread stuffing is undoubtedly delicious and nostalgic, but what if we switched it up a bit this year and tried something new? Enter: flaky, savory-sweet croissant stuffing.

This recipe is for everyone who hates marshmallows atop their sweet potato casserole—in their place is a buttery, brown sugar pecan topping that is still perfectly sweet and Thanksgiving-worthy.

Packed with sweet corn, balanced by a pinch of paprika and herby chives, this fall casserole has an insanely tender and custardy texture that will have you on your third helping before you even know what hit you. Let this classic side be the star of your Thanksgiving dinner if you’re ever in the mood for endless praise and compliments.

According to recent reports, whether you’re drizzling it over your roast turkey, mashed potatoes, or flaky biscuits, homemade gravy is an absolute must-have during the holidays. Since it’s such a staple, it's gotta be perfect—THIS is the recipe you need.

There is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. You can use sweet potato puree from a can, or if you have leftover baked sweet potato, you can use that as well.

Sources indicate that what do you get when you take mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf? Million-dollar mac. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food in a casserole will take center stage on any table it hits.

Onion Soup Mix Roasted Potatoes.

If you love stovetop mac 'n' cheese on your Thanksgiving table, you’ve got to try this creamy butternut squash orzo. Butternut squash and Parmesan join forces with orzo to create a cheesy pasta skillet that hits every nostalgic note.

#111906. Ballerina Farm Is Opening a Restaurant, Farm Store, and Cooking School—Here’s a First Look

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2409 w)

Ballerina Farm Is Opening a Restaurant, Farm Store, and Cooking School—Here’s a First Look

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s a glorious late-September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me.
  • In a recent development, still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me.
  • He speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s a glorious late-September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me. A soft breeze hints at the seasonal shift that will soon blanket this bucolic corner of Utah in frost. I’m standing beside two of Daniel Neeleman’s daughters and Daniel himself, his head full of curly hair and his feet tucked into work boots. He exudes the easy familiarity of an old friend, despite a family name—and now a social media presence, thanks to Ballerina Farm’s 20 million–plus combined followers—that has taken on a life of its own.

In a recent development, still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me. “We love small agriculture and the diversification of it,” he states. “I think that we can make an impact in helping people see that small agriculture can work. Whether you’re doing an agritourism aspect or not, we still think it should and can be profitable.”.

He speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America. Daniel did not grow up with animals and still remembers how mesmerized he was the first time he saw a cow. “I tell people on the farm tours all the time, if your endorphins are going off watching these animals, watch out. You might be a farmer. It doesn’t go away—it might come back to you later in life.” From the very day that Daniel and his now famous wife, Hannah, bought their first farm in 2017, he knew this was where they were meant to be.

Earlier that morning, I was sitting at their kitchen dining table over a brunch of quiche, greens, yogurt, and tea made from just-picked mint, the spread illuminated by beeswax spindle candles. “It’s our responsibility, and our love and passion too, to build this,” Hannah tells me, wearing a white dress with three daughters by her side. She’s sitting against a backdrop that’s become familiar to millions who have watched her cook and feed her growing family on a farm less than an hour outside Salt Lake City.

Despite their sincere intentions, the Neelemans’ endeavor has brought moments of global controversy. The internet has scrutinized their approach to homeschooling their nine children, their family wealth, and how they balance their roles as parents and cofounders. “We don’t take the platform that we’ve been given lightly,” Hannah says. Agriculture, she explains, has been at the heart of the project from the beginning, even as its reach has expanded far beyond the Kamas Valley. “It has worn a lot of different hats as it’s grown. We were young city kids, and we craved something real and knowing where our food comes from.”.

In a recent development, now, what began as a story told online is becoming a universe people can actually step into. On a stretch of land that spreads out beyond the window like something from “America the Beautiful,” they’re planning—and here announcing—one of the country’s most ambitious upcoming farm hospitality destinations: a cookery school, farm-to-table restaurant, farm store, and spaces for agricultural education and events, all set within a working farm encompassing livestock, organic gardens, a dairy, and a forthcoming creamery.

According to recent reports, at the heart of the vision is a cookery school, scheduled to open in 2029, that is as much about learning to cook from the farm as it is about taking those lessons home. The goal is to teach people how to cook seasonally and adapt when certain ingredients aren’t available, wherever they might live. (Daniel describes this as an education in life skills rather than formal chef training.) “I want students to have time with the dairy, the market garden, the creamery, so they’re seeing where the food comes from,” Hannah notes.

The cookery school will be guided by a philosophy similar to that of the legendary Ballymaloe Cookery School, where Hannah and Daniel spent 12 weeks in 2025—and first met Michael “Tiffin” Griffin, a beloved longtime instructor who has since joined Ballerina Farm as the director of the culinary experience. (A more formal, fine-dining restaurant may eventually complement the school.).

But visitors can step into the newly introduced Ballerina Farm world as soon as fall 2027, when a Dutch barn is slated to open at the site of the current Kamas market. Inside will be a restaurant and café, which the couple collectively calls an “eatery,” serving meals featuring the meat, dairy, and produce grown on the surrounding farm—a considerable expansion of the current menus at the Midway store and food truck.

In a recent development, across a breezeway, a market will offer fresh produce straight from the garden and meat and dairy from the livestock—think onions, pea shoots, beets, rib-eye steaks, smoked paprika goat cheese, and gallons of A2/A2 cream-top whole milk—as well as a growing selection of prepared sides, sauces, and meals, from pickled torpedo onions to just-juiced turmeric ginger shots to chicken salad. The latter is Hannah’s particular favorite. “We got so attached to the chicken salad that we had this summer, because we grew meat chickens. We harvested them. And they made the most delicious chicken salad. Then Tiffin told us this week, ‘One more week of the chicken salad—I’m out of pickles. You’ll see it next spring.’ And I went, ‘Nooo.’” She laughs. “I think people are getting back to how grandma used to cook. She cooked from the garden, and it was amazing food.”.

Just-cut spinach and radishes will sit next to Ballerina Farm’s signature products, initially available only online, as well as Ballerina Farm’s home goods like oven mitts, aprons, and wooden measuring spoons, with the name appearing only discreetly. They also released their first skin-care product just this month: Tallow Tin body butter—made with tallow from the cattle, naturally.

The restaurant, farm store, and connecting courtyard will be more than five times the size of the existing Ballerina Farm store and café that opened in 2025, 25 minutes down the road in Midway. “There’s an awful lot of hullabaloo about Hannah doing it, but for me that’s what I saw when I was a kid,” Tiffin, the culinary director, tells me. “That’s how my grandmother lived her life.”.

Over a two-hour meal of Ballerina Farm roasted chicken, garden carrots, pickled onions, and homemade yogurt, I sat enraptured by Tiffin’s story and the depth of knowledge and experience that had brought him to this particular farm in Utah. While guests can expect a diversity of dishes—Tiffin is especially passionate about Moroccan flavors—the land is the final decision maker. “We’ll ask Tiffin what’s on the menu for an event,” Daniel explains, “and the first thing he’ll say is, ‘Let me call Madison [Goodman], the head grower.’”.

Goodman is responsible for a vegetable operation that will eventually expand to five acres. The kitchen will draw on its harvest but supplement it with neighboring producers when necessary—a philosophy similar to that which guided Tiffin at Ballymaloe: “If we can’t grow it, we get it locally. If we can’t get it locally, we’ll get the best.”.

According to recent reports, the design and architecture of the project, meanwhile, will be led by Patrick Williams of Berdoulat, the British design house known for its richly textured, historically informed interiors. At Berdoulat, the mantra is “the house rules.” But as Williams puts it, “In this instance, where the buildings are yet to exist, the land rules.” His designs draw inspiration from 19th-century settlers’ homes and agricultural buildings in the Kamas Valley (and, yes, the family’s famous farmstead).

Sources indicate that the Ballerina Farm team has worked closely with Kamas officials for years now to define what can be developed on its 14-acre property, prompting the city to introduce new agritourism zoning in 2024. The prepares also protect the property’s conserved wetlands. “We are constantly in touch with the city,” says Brad Roberts, the brand’s director of marketing. If done well, Kamas can become a role model for the many other small towns grappling with their own decisions around the opportunities made possible through agritourism.

Yet the Kamas Valley is not the most obvious place to craft such an ambitious project that’s certain to draw travelers not only from the coasts but also from overseas. (Eighty percent of Ballerina Farm’s 10 million–plus Instagram following is based outside of the US.) A high water table can flood the gardens, frosts set in as early as October, and voles relentlessly try to work their way into the harvest. But the valley has a certain quality of light, giant skies, and an openness that feels rarer than ever in today’s world.

Walking through three high tunnels filled to the brim with produce, I eventually met Goodman, a fourth-generation farmer who ran his own successful community-supported agriculture program in the Kamas Valley and was courted for years by the Neelemans before joining the Ballerina Farm team. He speaks passionately about the farm’s recently earned USDA organic certification and the decades of advocacy that brought those standards into existence. “You can make me cry, because there are a lot of people who fought hard for this,” Goodman says, describing the certification’s baseline standards as the floor while emphasizing that he’s reaching for the ceiling. “The label helps us bridge this gap that we, as a society, have created between our reality.”.

Sources indicate that he continues: “Everything here has a story. I can tell you the story of the winter leek. I can tell you the story of these girls.” (The girls are chickens.) He then spends 10 minutes explaining to me exactly why these chickens—Freedom Rangers rather than the more commonly raised Cornish Cross—are so special and how they’re raised from chicks to harvest. “It’s hard for me to do this and not believe in a creator,” Goodman says.

According to recent reports, one of the challenges and opportunities of an agritourism project is that, in a four-season destination like Utah, the experience will be remarkably different depending on when visitors arrive: tomatoes in the summer, spinach in the winter, chicks in one season, and a mature flock in another. “There’s something beautiful about eating what’s in season and retraining us as eaters to appreciate that,” Hannah reflects. “I have started to notice that I’m craving spinach, pumpkin, and squash because your body wants the things that are growing.”.

The culture side of agriculture has probably played a larger role in the Neelemans’ agricultural pursuits than they expected, however. While Hannah started sharing on social media as a way to kick-start business for their nascent pork operation, it snowballed into a public inquisition over what many perceived as an idealized, regressive performance of rural domesticity. But what the public wanted to know most was how it was possible. What was real? And who funded it?

Industry observers note that when I ask them about balancing their ambitious vision with the realities of building a farm and business, Hannah claims, “That’s a true founder of a manufacturer. They are the one who has to hold those two worlds together. We have to keep the dreams alive and the fire burning, but we’re also camping over the farm stand or dealing with broken pipes and trying to put up hoop houses.”.

Sources indicate that daniel adds: “We’re the ones that decide whenever there’s money left over at the end of the month from the business.” He notes that every individual part of the business is profitable. “We don’t have any investors, we don’t have any partners—it’s just us. So then it’s just a question of, What projects are we going to conquer first? We are a for-profit firm, and we have to be good stewards of the finances of all the things. It has to be sustainable.”.

For years, people have been asking to visit, Hannah explains, sending her messages asking to meet the animals, help with chores, or simply spend a day on the farm. At the time, the Neelemans weren’t equipped to receive this audience of millions who had developed a relationship with a place they’d never visited. Now, they’re preparing to welcome both admirers and curious outsiders, as well as farmers and cooks, into the world that has generated so much conversation. “We have a community that wants to be a part of it,” Hannah recalls thinking. “So how do we build it?”.

This newly introduced expression of Ballerina Farm places Hannah and Daniel among a lineage of visionaries in farm hospitality who have transformed working farms into gathering places—Ballymaloe, yes, but also Daylesford Organic in the English Cotswolds and Babylonstoren in South Africa. But of course, one notable factor sets Ballerina Farm’s journey apart. Rather than building a hospitality destination and then finding an audience, the Neelemans are working the other way around. The relationship is already shaped by years of watching the family’s life unfold online—and by the very different ideas people have formed about what Ballerina Farm represents.

It’s easy to understand the appeal: Rather than watch a 60-second video on their phones, visitors can pull sourdough or slip on a Ballerina Farm oven mitt and slide a pork chop out of the oven. They can greet a just-born calf. Their children can run the fields, breathe the fresh Utah air, and taste the milk from Daniel’s cows. As I pulled through the gates of Ballerina Farm in my rental car and watched six Sebastopol geese waddle in front of me, even I felt that very modern feeling of disorienting familiarity upon experiencing a person or a place in the flesh that I had only ever seen on a screen.

Right now, the Kamas property has already begun hosting farm dinners, seasonal events, and agricultural experiences alongside the market and food truck. Each offering showcases how the Ballerina Farm world will eventually come together: market, meals, events, education, animals, and gardens all in one place.

Sources indicate that and for all the ambition of what Hannah and Daniel are building, the idea at its heart remains deeply personal. “The greatest work that we can do is in our homes and our own families and our communities,” Hannah tells me, a conviction that has remained constant even as Ballerina Farm’s audience has rapidly grown.

Adds Daniel, “We’ve accomplished some things that we’re proud of, but we’re far from being done.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you initiative to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

It has been revealed that we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Sources indicate that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

In a recent development, whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

It has been revealed that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

According to recent reports, place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Sources indicate that transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Industry observers note that spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#111899. Latest Update: Veruschka, the Shape-Shifting Supermodel Who Defined an Era, Has Died at 87

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (986 w)

Latest Update: Veruschka, the Shape-Shifting Supermodel Who Defined an Era, Has Died at 87

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Richard Avedon famously pronounced Veruschka “the most beautiful woman in the world.” But what made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty.
  • On November 25 it was confirmed by the German newspaper Bild that the model died at the age of 87, surrounded by friends and family at home.
  • It was only earlier this month, on the occasion of the release of Ron Howard’s Netflix documentary Avedon, that Vogue revisited an extraordinary 25-page fashion editorial from its March 1, 1967, matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Richard Avedon famously pronounced Veruschka “the most beautiful woman in the world.” But what made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty. She could be imperious or impish, feral or feline, androgynous or opulently feminine. She could contort her impossibly long limbs into unreal configurations, traversing fashion magazines and the wider public’s consciousness with ease in a way that had never been done before. One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion’s great performance artists.

On November 25 it was confirmed by the German newspaper Bild that the model died at the age of 87, surrounded by friends and family at home.

It was only earlier this month, on the occasion of the release of Ron Howard’s Netflix documentary Avedon, that Vogue revisited an extraordinary 25-page fashion editorial from its March 1, 1967, matter. Across those pages, Veruschka leapt and pirouetted, her hair fashioned into a long, swinging braid by hairstylist Ara Gallant. Avedon had found in Veruschka a woman who could give physical expression to his imagination and whose own imagination was every bit as expansive. Here was a woman whose beauty “demands something, and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever,” stated Avedon.

It has been revealed that born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia), Veruschka’s early life was marked by the horrors of war. She was five years old when her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed for his involvement in the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. The family was imprisoned by the Nazi regime, and the aristocratic world into which she had been born had all but disappeared by the time the war came to an end.

An art student, she was discovered in Florence in 1959. Her early forays into modeling were not immediately fruitful: Standing over six feet tall, she was an unconventional proposition even then. An initial stint in New York proved disappointing, but in Italy she developed a fruitful creative relationship with photographer Johnny Moncada. Some 3,000 images from those formative years, undiscovered for decades, would eventually form the basis of the book From Vera to Veruschka: The Unseen Photographs by Johnny Moncada and an accompanying exhibition at London’s Somerset House in 2014.

Her greatest act of reinvention was, arguably, the creation of Veruschka herself. Adopting the Russian-sounding diminutive of her first name, she cultivated a persona of indeterminate provenance and mystique. Returning to Upcoming York in 1964, she found an industry increasingly receptive to her brand of beauty. In Diana Vreeland, then editor in chief of Vogue, she found a kindred spirit.

In a recent development, the 1960s heralded the ascendance of a new breed of model, with the likes of Jean Shrimpton, Twiggy, Donyale Luna, and Penelope Tree becoming cultural figures in their own right. Veruschka, with her high forehead, sculptural cheekbones, and elongated limbs, was one of the decade’s most arresting presences, whatever aesthetic she took on. She appeared on 13 American Vogue covers, working with the likes of Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst, and David Bailey, and became one of the highest-paid models of her generation.

It has been revealed that some of her most enduring images were made in collaboration with the Italian photographer Franco Rubartelli, her creative and romantic partner. Among them was the indelible 1968 photograph of Veruschka in Yves Saint Laurent’s lace-up safari jacket for French Vogue, an image that distilled the designer’s upcoming vocabulary of female sensuality and authority.

Veruschka was also an endlessly inventive beauty muse. The Vogue archives are rich with examples of her aesthetic adventurism. She sports fantastical lashes, intricately braided hair, graphic eye makeup, and elaborate headpieces. She was chameleonic, which made her popular with the hair and makeup artists of the era.

And her fame extended well beyond the pages of fashion magazines. In Michelangelo Antonioni’s seminal 1966 film Blow-Up, set in Swinging London, Veruschka played a version of herself in a brief but electrifying scene opposite David Hemmings’s fashion photographer. A year later, she graced the cover of Life magazine. Few models before her had so thoroughly captured the imagination of the wider public, and her legacy lives on in the upcoming generation of celebrity models today.

By the mid-1970s, however, Veruschka had grown disenchanted with the fashion industry. Her artistic ambitions began to take greater precedence over her modeling career. In collaboration with the German artist Holger Trülzsch, she embarked on a captivating body of photographic work in which her painted figure dissolved into architectural surfaces and natural environments, or assumed entirely different identities.

It has been revealed that in 1971 Veruschka also appeared in West German magazine Stern with 27 other women under the coverline: “Wir haben abgetrieben!” (“We’ve had abortions!”) to advocate for abortion law reform at a time when it was illegal. It was a significant moment in Germany’s ’70s feminist wave.

It has been revealed that still, fashion never entirely relinquished its fascination with her, nor she with it. There were occasional returns to the runway, including for Chanel in 1994 and, at the age of 71, for Giles Deacon’s spring 2011 show in London. In 2017, Acne Studios enlisted her for its resort 2018 look book. In contemporary photos—with her silver hair slicked back, sporting oversized, louche tailoring—she looks every bit as modern as she had half a century earlier.

Veruschka on the red carpet at the Berlin Film Festival in 2015.

Much has been made of Veruschka’s otherworldliness, but there was something profoundly human in her commitment to metamorphosis. At the height of her fame, she could have made a career out of being the most beautiful woman in the world. How much more interesting, instead, to become a thousand different women.

#111898. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that with only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished.
  • Sources indicate that the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder.
  • Industry observers note that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

Sources indicate that the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, states of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

Industry observers note that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

It has been revealed that the Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman indicates this fresh outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Sources indicate that whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman indicates. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she states.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she states. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up rapidly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Veruschka, the legendary German model who helped revolutionize fashion photography during the late 1960s and early ’70s, has died at the age of 87, a family member confirmed to the German newspaper Bild.

The statuesque beauty was known for her collaborations with the leading photographers of her day—Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, and Bert Stern among them—and many of her most enduring shoots were originally published within the pages of Vogue. It was the magazine’s visionary editor in chief Diana Vreeland who famously championed the six-foot-one newcomer after discovering her in Paris and urging her to drop her aristocratic surname, recognizing her as a perfect conduit for the era’s psychedelic, boundary-pushing spirit.

As a result, she appeared on the cover of the magazine some 12 times. In the year of 1965 alone, she was a Vogue cover star on five separate occasions. Seen together, they serve as a remarkable document of fashion’s seismic shifts throughout the 1960s, her endless versatility as a model, and the remarkable alchemy she shared with many of the era’s most extraordinary image makers.

Sources indicate that whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Sources indicate that turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

According to recent reports, when dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

According to recent reports, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

It has been revealed that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

(If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

There are few faces more synonymous with the youthquake of the ’60s than Veruschka, who has sadly passed away at the age of 87.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort in East Prussia, the German countess was discovered at 20 years old while studying art in Florence. Soon after, she decamped to Fresh York City, where she changed her name from Vera to Veruschka and became one of the most—if not the most—in-demand supermodels of the decade, regularly appearing in the pages of Vogue and lensed by greats such as David Bailey, Irving Penn, and Richard Avedon.

Recent findings suggest that standing six feet tall, she was a bombshell with a chiseled-by-the-gods bone structure, steely blue gaze, plush mouth, and shape-shifting champagne-blonde hair. Her “indomitable career of beauty,” as Susan Sontag once famously deemed it, was characterized by portraits of her sinewy silhouette, immortalized most notoriously in that scene from Michelangelo Antonioni’s cult 1966 film Blow-Up, where she poses for photographer David Hemmings’s camera to amorous effect.

As for her countless evocative close-ups, which showcased her otherworldly hair and makeup looks, nothing was too decorative or directional for Veruschka, and it was this perpetual gameness that made her a favorite of Diana Vreeland during her tenure at Vogue. There were her sculptural, teased-to-the-heavens, and decidedly ’60s hair looks, from a voluminous bouffant with waist-grazing lengths, to an origami-like knot, to the tornado of face-framing braids that she wore in a 1967 editorial shot by her longtime lover and collaborator Franco Rubartelli. And then there were her signature extreme lashes, which ran the gamut from classic, doll-like fringe to cast in Technicolor shades or granddaddy longlegs lengths, and were often punctuated by a sheer wash of pastel pigment on the lids, graphic winged liner, and glossy pink lips.

It has been revealed that “The most beautiful woman in the world,” according to Avedon, and a true chameleon in every sense of the word, Veruschka’s metamorphic fluency continues to be a lethal and enduring combination in the fashion world. In fact, in 2017, Acne Studios tapped Veruschka to star in its Resort 2018 look book, where she wore the collection’s cropped jackets and slouchy trousers with a sharp slick back and statuesque swagger. Here, a look at her most striking beauty looks of all time.

#111883. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Gravy-Braised Turkey

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment.
  • Industry observers note that this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

Industry observers note that this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first crucial step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

Recent findings suggest that add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

In a recent development, nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Sources indicate that let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

This Is What Was on the Menu at the First Thanksgiving in 1621

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.
  • For a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate.
  • The gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.

For a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate. We know there were roughly 140 people, three days of feasting and exactly five deer. Beyond that, the historical record is rather unhelpful. Apparently, nobody thought to write down the menu.

The gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit. It was a meeting between two communities whose relationship was far more complicated than the cheerful scene that would eventually find its way into American classrooms. Although they had formed an alliance earlier that year, cultural differences and tensions of an English settlement on Wampanoag land were hardly going to disappear over dinner.

In a recent development, and while the English had much to celebrate in bringing in their first harvest, they owed a great deal of that success to Indigenous knowledge. The Wampanoag understood the region’s growing seasons, its waterways and the foods that could be grown and gathered in the surrounding landscape. Their traditions had helped sustain communities there long before the colonists arrived.

The two surviving English accounts of the gathering offer only a few details about the feast itself, but taken together with what historians know about the food traditions of both communities, they give us a rather interesting picture of what may have been on the table.

Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists who attended the gathering, recorded that the Wampanoag went hunting and returned with five deer, which they presented to the colony’s leaders. It’s one of the few specific foods mentioned in his account and an especially substantial contribution to a celebration that lasted three days.

Recent findings suggest that deer were an important source of food for the Wampanoag, who also made use of their hides, bones and other materials. In England, however, deer hunting was largely reserved for the wealthy, making venison something most ordinary people rarely got to enjoy. The meat may have been roasted over a fire or simmered in a hearty venison stew, although Winslow neglected to tell us how it was prepared. We know exactly how many deer arrived, but what became of them in the kitchen remains a mystery.

In a recent development, roast turkey has become so thoroughly associated with Thanksgiving that it’s difficult to imagine the holiday without one occupying the center of the table. The trouble is, we don’t actually know whether turkey was served at the original celebration.

In a recent development, winslow wrote that four Englishmen went hunting for wildfowl and returned with enough to feed the colonists for nearly a week. What he didn’t do was tell us which birds they shot. Wild turkeys were present in the region, but so were ducks, geese and other game birds, all perfectly suitable for roasting over a fire. There’s every possibility that turkey was on the menu, but nothing to suggest it enjoyed the distinction we’ve since bestowed upon it. For all we know, the centerpiece was a duck, and we’ve spent the last few centuries giving credit to the wrong bird.

Corn was one of the most vital foods available to both communities, although the English were relatively newly introduced to growing it. The Wampanoag had cultivated maize for generations, developing agricultural practices suited to the region’s soil and growing seasons. Their knowledge was enormously valuable to the colonists, whose first attempts at establishing a food supply had been anything but fruitful.

One traditional Wampanoag preparation was nasaump, a thick porridge made from ground corn, sometimes cooked with other ingredients. Corn could also be ground into meal for simple breads, early relatives of the cornbread we bake today, or used to thicken stews and make other hearty dishes.

The waters around Plymouth were full of food, provided you knew where to look and how to catch it. The Wampanoag had long fished the region’s rivers and coastline, gathering shellfish and catching everything from bass and cod to eels. Clams, mussels and lobsters were plentiful too.

The English were beginning to take advantage of these resources by 1621. William Bradford, the Plymouth colony’s governor, wrote of the colonists catching substantial quantities of cod and bass during the summer. A freshly caught fish could be roasted or boiled, while clams and mussels might be cooked over a fire. Lobster was another plentiful local catch that was enjoyed regularly. The variety of ocean fare available might have made for a Thanksgiving spread that looked rather more like a seafood boil than the feast we know today.

Industry observers note that squash and pumpkin were crucial crops in Wampanoag agriculture, and their ability to keep well after harvest made them especially useful as the colder weather set in. Both could be roasted, boiled or added to stews, much like we still prepare winter squash today, though without the benefit of a balsamic glaze.

In a recent development, the English called pumpkins pompions, a name I think we abandoned prematurely. They were familiar with the vegetable, although the varieties growing in New England differed from those they might have seen at home. A pumpkin dish would have been entirely plausible at the harvest celebration, but anyone hoping for a slice of pumpkin pie would have to wait almost two centuries. The colonists had limited supplies of wheat flour, butter and sugar, and the familiar custard-filled pie wouldn’t appear in American cookbooks until 1796.

The Wampanoag grew beans alongside corn and squash, three crops that complemented each other remarkably well. Cornstalks supported climbing beans, while squash vines spread across the ground and helped shade the soil. The combination was as useful in the garden as it was on the plate.

Sources indicate that A traditional Wampanoag stew called sobaheg combines ingredients like corn, beans, squash and meat or fish, depending on what’s available or in season. The combination of corn and beans also appears in succotash, another dish with Indigenous Newly introduced England roots that remains an American favorite.

It has been revealed that the forests and wetlands of Newly introduced England offered plenty beyond cultivated crops. Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, wild grapes and cranberries were among the foods the Wampanoag knew how to gather and prepare, each with its own season and uses.

Nuts could be eaten plain, stored or ground into meal, while fruits could be enjoyed fresh or preserved for later. Acorns required particular attention, since their natural bitterness had to be leached out with water before they could be used in cooking. It’s one of the few ingredients we’ve more or less surrendered entirely to the squirrels.

Recent findings suggest that of all the wild fruits available, cranberries have perhaps the most recognizable place on a modern Thanksgiving table. Their natural tartness eventually found a friend in sugar, giving rise to the cranberry sauce that’s become nearly as much a part of the holiday as the turkey itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Sources indicate that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

This Is Why Your Mashed Potatoes Are Gluey (and How to Fix It)

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • My mom’s potato masher is one of my favorite kitchen tools, from its retro design to the thick, grid-patterned bottom that hasn’t bent or warped over the years, despite heavy use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Consider this your mashed potato primer, complete with tips on how to fix gluey mashed potatoes and how to prevent them from the start.

My mom’s potato masher is one of my favorite kitchen tools, from its retro design to the thick, grid-patterned bottom that hasn’t bent or warped over the years, despite heavy use. I attributed her consistently perfect fluffy mashed potatoes to this simple tool, even when she was experimenting with latest mashed potato ideas. And it turns out there is some truth to it because it created smooth mashed potatoes quickly yet thoroughly, preventing her from pummeling the spuds into a sticky, gummy mess.

You see, overworked potatoes are the biggest reason for gluey mashed potatoes, so using the right tool is the best way to prevent them in the first place. And if you came here because your potatoes are already gummy, we have some helpful tips for how to fix gluey mashed potatoes after the fact.

Sources indicate that the biggest culprit for gluey mashed potatoes is overworked potatoes. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and a little bit of starch is a good thing. Just as aquafaba (starchy cooked chickpea liquid) can be whipped into a rich vegan mayonnaise, potato starch thickens mashed potatoes and contributes to a creamy texture. But there is a limit.

As you mash chunks of potatoes into a mostly smooth mixture, the spud’s cell walls collapse, freeing the starch within those cells. The more you mash, the more cells are broken down, and the thicker, starchier and gummier the potatoes become. This can happen when you mash potatoes too long by hand, but it happens more quickly when using electric tools.

Industry observers note that food processors and immersion blenders have incredibly fast, sharp blades. As they whip around, they cut through the potatoes’ cells so rapidly that the once silken mash becomes gluey in a flash. I can’t urge you strongly enough to pass on these tools when mashing potatoes.

There are three components to avoiding gluey mashed potatoes: Choosing the right potato, using the right tool and considering temperature.

In a recent development, for starters, choose a starchy or all-purpose potato, like a russet or Yukon Gold. These potatoes are relatively low in moisture, helping the potato break down into a creamy mixture. They’ll give you more wiggle room as you mash than waxy potatoes, so the potatoes will turn out delicious even if you lose yourself in exuberant mashing.

Recent findings suggest that next, use the right kitchen tool for the job and reach for a potato masher, food mill or ricer. These handheld tools give you more control over speed and power as you mash. I prefer a potato masher with a crisscross grid pattern over those with a wavy design because there’s less open space, making each mash more productive.

Finally, warm your butter and milk before adding them to the potatoes. This step may sound finicky, but it prevents the warm potato starches from seizing against cold ingredients and becoming dense. Switch to a spatula and stir them in to keep a gentle touch and retain a fluffy texture.

Industry observers note that you’ll never be able to totally remove the excess starch and get rid of the gluey texture without starting over, but you may be able to improve it. Adding more fat or liquid can improve the mouthfeel, and stirring in other ingredients can alter the overall texture.

If your potatoes are truly a gluey mess, don’t fret; you can repurpose the potatoes by turning them into leftover mashed potato recipes. Here are some of my favorite ways to use gluey mashed potatoes:.

Knowing what types of potatoes are best for which recipes can save you a lot of grief—and this knowledge will go a long way to preventing gluey potatoes. For the creamiest, smoothest, lightest-as-air mashed potatoes, go with a starchy russet potato. Some people like using all-purpose Yukon Gold potatoes for their naturally buttery flavor, but I prefer to use all russets (or a blend of russets and Yukon Golds for flavor).

It’s best to avoid waxy potatoes, like red or fingerling potatoes, for mashed potato recipes. They keep their shape when they’re cooked, which is why they’re better for potato salads and soups than creamy mashes. They do make an excellent smashed potato, though, if you’re looking to do something a little bit different with your side dish.

According to recent reports, as with all cooking rules, this one is made to be broken. If you only have red potatoes in the pantry, you can still use them to make mashed red potatoes. Just keep the potatoes a little bit chunkier so they don’t get gummy. And make sure you refer to them as a “rustic” mash when you bring them to the table to properly temper expectations.

Can Your Home Boost Your Endorphins? 7 Simple Tips for a Healthier, Happier Living Space

💡 Key Takeaways
