  • Here are seven practical tips to help create a home environment that helps boost your mental and physical health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on a recent cold Sunday morning, I had no interest in doing anything except hiding from the world. Then I did a few small tasks that completely shifted my mood. First, I spritzed a home fragrance with notes of orange and cinnamon around my apartment; next, I raised the blinds to let in some sunlight and tidied up the living room—clearing away clutter, folding blankets, and fluffing the pillows on the couch. As I did, I recalled the words of Loewe’s perfumer, Nuria Cruelles, about one of her candles: “It has the power to transform your house into a home.” That’s exactly what I was doing, simply by adding a bit of scent and straightening up. Another expert, Dr. Rodrigo Arteaga, explains that anyone can turn their home into a “place that improves their health” by following a few simple habits.

Recent findings suggest that there are indeed many small routines we can adopt to turn our home—the place where we relax and let our guard down—into an environment that fosters well-being. Psychologist María Martínez echoes this, encouraging people to practice the Japanese philosophy of kaizen, which emphasizes the transformative power of making gradual, continuous improvements to our lives. “It’s important to create an environment where you look around and like what you see,” she says. “This releases endorphins and makes you feel good. If instead, everywhere you look, there’s a reminder of a task you need to do, something unattractive, or clutter that causes stress, you’ll end up feeling worse. If it gets bad enough, you’ll soon stop wanting to be in your own home. You’ll find reasons to leave or stay late at the office, coming home only to sleep. These are all signs that you need to make changes—not just in your life, but in your home, which should serve as a sanctuary where you can recharge.”.

Here are seven practical tips to help create a home environment that helps boost your mental and physical health.

According to recent reports, when Florence Pugh was asked in a recent Vogue interview what a perfect day off looks like for her, one of the first things she mentioned was buying flowers. “I love going to my florist and putting together a beautiful bouquet; it makes me so happy,” she said. She’s not alone. According to a study by Dr. Nancy Etcoff of Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, flowers ward off worry, anxiety, and sadness. Study participants felt noticeably better after having flowers in their homes for just a few days—and tended to place them in the kitchen, dining room, and living room, the spaces where they spent most of their time.

Whenever possible, open your curtains and blinds in the morning. As Dr. Arteaga points out, “This gives your brain a powerful signal to synchronize its biological clock. Natural light helps your body recognize when it’s day and when it’s night, giving you more energy during the daytime and helping you rest better at night.” After dusk, create “light islands” inspired by the Danish philosophy of hygge, which offers plenty of ideas for designing a wellness-focused home. As Meik Wiking explains in his book My Hygge Home, you can bring warmth to dark corners of a living room using lamps that cast light downward and bulbs that emit a soft, warm glow. Floor or table lamps placed near a sofa or reading chair work especially well. For more general lighting in spaces meant for relaxation, hygge experts recommend ceiling or wall fixtures with glass or fabric shades that diffuse light gently, rather than harsh overhead chandeliers or pendants.

Studies show that listening to music you love provides an immediate boost to your well-being. “Music has an instant, almost magical effect on us,” explains psychologist Marta Calderero. “Within just a few seconds of hearing a favorite song, your brain is flooded with endorphins and oxytocin. That’s why you suddenly feel that rush of euphoria and such an intimate connection to a track. And it doesn’t stop there—after a couple of minutes, the brain begins releasing dopamine, making us enjoy each second a little more than the last. It’s the most beautiful way I know to regulate emotions and reconnect with the present moment.”.

Hygge inspired another recommendation on our list. As Wiking explains, styling a small corner of your home with cozy lighting, blankets (a hygge staple), pillows, a plush rug, and a few favorite objects creates a dedicated spot to unplug from the world. It’s a simple way to build an inviting nook that signals to your brain that you’re in a safe space where it’s okay to relax and unwind.

It has been revealed that going barefoot indoors is another of Dr. Arteaga’s recommendations, and Beatriz Crespo, an expert in healthy micro-habits, seconds the idea. Beyond its physical perks—like improved circulation and balance—walking barefoot reduces stress and encourages relaxation through direct contact between the ground and the nerve-rich soles of your feet.

Proper ventilation offers clear microbiological benefits, as biologist María Dolores Cima Cabal explains: “It helps reduce the density of microorganisms that accumulate inside the home.” At the same time, it delivers real psychological perks, since breathing fresh air reenergizes the body and supplies oxygen to the brain. A Harvard University study confirms that cognitive function can suffer—and reaction times slow down—in stuffy environments.

Sources indicate that returning to that chilly Sunday morning at the start of this piece, candles have a unique ability to turn a house into a home through the evocative power of scent. When you choose an appealing fragrance—whether as a room spray or a candle—your brain registers it as a cue that you’re somewhere you can let your guard down. “Smell is the sense that most powerfully triggers memories, and the one our brain responds to with the greatest intensity,” concludes Calderero. “It forms a direct link between a scent and an emotion. If you keep a signature scent at home, that olfactory connection becomes so strong that the moment you smell it, your brain associates it with rest, comfort, and warmth. Choosing a specific fragrance helps your brain recognize that it’s in a space where it doesn’t need to stay on high alert—and your nervous system naturally slows down.”.

Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind.
  • In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp.
  • Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

More showstopping cabbage recipes here.

In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

Make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

It has been revealed that while the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

Make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

When the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Drizzle generously with hot sauce, letting it seep into the leaves. Finish with the golden breadcrumbs, fresh dill fronds, and a few extra grates of lemon zest. Serve immediately.

The Luxury Business of Las Vegas F1 Is Booming

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If Formula 1 circuits were Mario Kart race tracks, the Las Vegas Grand Prix is as spiritually close to Rainbow Road as it gets.

According to recent reports, this year, newly hybrid-engined F1 cars zoomed along an LED-lit Vegas Strip that had been closed off to civilian traffic each night of the event, much to the chagrin of every ride-share driver and/or tourist trying to cross Las Vegas Boulevard. They whipped past the Paris hotel casino’s glittering facsimile of the Eiffel Tower and the cartoonishly massive Sphere. They skirted under banners advertising Louis Vuitton and Qatar Airways. At the end, winner Max Verstappen was driven in a racing-striped stretch limousine, operated by a dashingly bedraggled Keanu Reeves, to the Fountains of Bellagio—inspired, like so many Vegas landmarks, by the architectural grandeur of Europe.

Max Verstappen, shortly after his win on Saturday night.

Motorsports enthusiast Keanu Reeves, center, drove the winners in a limo.

It has been revealed that since the Vegas GP was first revived in 2023, it has been a polarizing stop on the globe-trotting F1 calendar. (Back then, Verstappen called it “99 percent show and 1 percent sporting event.”) Even for a multibillion-dollar sport, was this too much glitz? Surrounded by sandy desert and snow-capped mountains, the gaudiest track in Formula 1 is nevertheless a sight to behold—and this year, it produced one of the most thrilling races in recent memory. Plus, as far as metropolises go, there are certainly more boring places to spend a few days than Sin City.

The winners’ podium: Red Bull’s Verstappen in first, followed by McLaren pair Lando Norris, left, and Oscar Piastri.

Well, unless you’re Kimi Antonelli, F1’s baby-faced world champ.

“The thing I like the most here is the track, because I’m not allowed to do anything else other than drive around,” Antonelli told me, with a smirk, ahead of the race last week. “Because I’m not 21.”.

(The Italian, who turned 20 in August, became Formula 1’s youngest-ever world champion at the Mexico Grand Prix earlier this month. In Vegas, he and his Mercedes teammate George Russell just missed the podium, finishing fourth and ninth respectively after more than a few late-race heartbreaks.).

Mercedes drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

It has been revealed that but if you’re too old to wait in the line outside Marquee, there were plenty of other desirable libations afoot. Vegas has always been a place where fine cuisine (or at least, high-roller cuisine) means bumping up prices by dumping truffles and caviar on everything. The OG greats of modern dining—the Jean-Georges Vongerichtens and Wolfgang Pucks—have been here since the ’90s. But since COVID, a latest generation of significant-brass restaurateurs have set up shop on the Strip: Carbone Riviera and the Corner Store at the Bellagio’s properties; Sartiano’s and Delilah at the Wynn; Mother Wolf and Contramar at the Fontainebleau. (There are elite members’ clubs, too: Zero Bond opened at the Wynn in March.).

Brunch at Sadelle's, a popular Major Food Group spot, inside the Bellagio.

Industry observers note that during Friday’s qualifying run, former F1 star Daniel Ricciardo stopped by the Corner Store at the Cosmopolitan, a wood-paneled outpost of the New York hotspot that opened a few weeks earlier. In the moody, multi-room space, the kitchen sends out platters of dry-aged wagyu and pepperoni pizza rolls while bartenders shake up sour-cream-and-onion martinis served with potato-chip sidecars. (The cocktail is purportedly Taylor Swift’s favorite, though executive chef Michael Vignola will neither confirm nor deny this: “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” stated Vignola, grinning. “You can also ask Travis.”).

A day earlier, Ricciardo—who retired from F1 last year but came to town for a self-branded clothing pop-up and bar at the Bellagio—reflected on his own experience at the first-reprised Vegas GP in 2023. “It feels like a video game,” he said. “Whether the track is your favorite or not your favorite in terms of the actual layout, it’s still pretty surreal to be here and be the main event in a city that revolves around entertainment.”.

According to Vignola, Ricciardo is a big fan of the Corner Store’s steak program as well as the chicken paillard, “a sleeper on the menu and a great mid-course this year.” Manning the kitchen at the Corner Store in Vegas, which has 100 more seats than the original NYC location, the chef said they’re selling about as much caviar here as they do in Manhattan.

“Because of the volume here, we are slightly selling a little bit more caviar, slightly, you know, maybe 2 to 1,” Vignola stated with a laugh. Lately, they’ve started R&D’ing some Norwegian king crab legs, including a prototype for a “crab appletini.” They’re leaning into menu items that the New York-born chef described as “a little bit more Vegas, flashy kind of bespoke things. There are some high-roller dishes that pop off.”.

An Elvis impersonator at F1's Paddock Club.

The likes of Vignola and Mario Carbone, as well as the actual Wolfgang Puck and Jean-Georges, hosted caviar-filled pop-up stands at the Bellagio Fountain Club suites during the F1 festivities. The starriest celebrities, including Reeves and Kim Kardashian, who’s dating driver Lewis Hamilton, watched the massive race from the paddock, with a good view of the Elvis impersonator and humanoid robots who roamed the asphalt.

Over my few days in Vegas, multiple locals—including chefs, service and casino employees, and Uber and Lyft drivers—described how the city’s changed over the last 15 years. On the ride from the airport, my driver pointed to a new landmark on the horizon: a massive mirrored edifice shaped like the body of a guitar (the new Hard Rock Las Vegas hotel) that’s in the midst of being erected from the sand.

Recent findings suggest that “I think Vegas and Formula 1, they were meant for each other,” said José Andrés, the Spanish-born chef who opened his first Las Vegas restaurants inside the then-freshly built Cosmopolitan in 2010. “I came here three weeks before the casino opened. And just to watch a casino open is the closest thing to watching a little egg hatch, or my daughter [being] born. For me to watch an entire casino from nothing to becoming a tower, it brings good memories.”.

One can only imagine how we’ll look back on the Las Vegas Grand Prix—only in its fourth year—a decade or two from now, when all the cars are self-driving and the Strip has been converted into an actual rainbow speedway floating in deep space. Will there still be Champagne?

I Learned How Baby Carrots Are Made & Haven't Bought Them Since—Here's Why

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a lover of all veggies, I love every type of carrot out there—except packaged baby carrots.
  • Here’s the truth about baby carrots—and why you might want to think twice about snagging a bag.
  • The bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a lover of all veggies, I love every type of carrot out there—except packaged baby carrots. That’s right: those bright orange cylinders with suspiciously perfect rounded corners that lurk in vending machines, school lunchboxes, and convenience store cold cases across our nation. They might be easy to eat on the go and better for you than a bag of Cheetos, but there’s a lot more going on behind the scenes of this seemingly simple healthy snack.

Here’s the truth about baby carrots—and why you might want to think twice about snagging a bag.

The bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size. Real baby carrots are immature carrots harvested before they reach full size. They’re sold in bunches—unpeeled, often with the tops still attached.

Recent findings suggest that while a whole carrot has a delicate, nuanced sweetness, the taste of these so-called baby carrots is best described as... factory-fresh. Don’t believe me? Grab a bag of regular carrots and do a side-by-side taste test.

Baby carrots were originally “invented” in the 1980s to make misshapen or broken carrots sellable. This was a smart way to reduce food waste and save money, but it also helped reinforce the unrealistic expectation that produce must look perfect in order to taste good. Today, baby-cut carrots are grown and processed to meet specific standards for size and shape, all to produce those identical little orange cylinders.

Here’s the bottom line: When you buy a bag of baby carrots, you’re buying into a world that’s seemingly as obsessed with unnatural perfection as the modern-day beauty industry.

In a recent development, energy conservation is top of mind for consumers these days, but making baby carrots look so uniform takes a lot of machinery. After they’re sorted, they chop the carrots into roughly 2-inch pieces and shave them—twice. Then, they go through a rough cutter, which gives them a general shape, before being polished to create those unrealistically perfect rounded edges. That’s a lot of extra work to make something that was completely edible to begin with look a certain way.

In a recent development, to prevent bacterial growth, baby carrots may be rinsed with a diluted chlorine solution before packaging. They’re then rinsed with water, and the chlorine treatment itself is an “acceptable” food-safety practice which doesn’t make baby carrots unsafe to eat. Still, do you really want your “fresh” snack to have undergone chlorine treatments of any kind? For me, that’s a hard no, and I’d rather buy whole carrots and wash and cut them myself.

Because baby carrots have been peeled and cut, they're more prone to drying out and developing something called “carrot blush,” a thin white film caused by dehydration. The film itself is harmless, but it certainly doesn’t make them look appetizing. Worse, they can turn slimy inside the bag, even before you open it. And that’s downright gross.

Prices vary depending on where you shop, but baby-cut carrots can cost more per pound than regular whole carrots. You're essentially paying extra for someone else to handle the peeling, cutting, and polishing. For a task that takes barely any time at home, I'd rather keep the difference in my wallet.

In a recent development, seriously. Enjoy the taste and texture of whole carrots, potentially save some money, and skip the extra processing by simply buying a bag of whole carrots and cutting them yourself. It’ll take you less time than you spent reading this article.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Brigadeiros are like a cross between fudge and Tootsie Rolls in truffle form. They're easy to make at home, and even easier to pop in your mouth.

As a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form. Brigadeiros have the familiar flavor and fudgy center of a really good chocolate truffle, but they’re even easier to make because they don’t require melting any chocolate. Everything happens in one small saucepan, and the only difficult part is waiting for the mixture to chill.

Sources indicate that brigadeiros start with a can of sweetened condensed milk, plus cocoa powder and butter. The butter is key to carrying the flavor of the cocoa powder and giving the bite-sized treats their signature soft bite. They end up as glossy little chocolate balls covered in sprinkles that taste halfway between a chocolate truffle and a piece of fudge: dense and chewy with a deep cocoa flavor and a center so creamy it nearly melts on contact.

It has been revealed that brigadeiros are Brazilian confections made by cooking a mixture of sweetened condensed milk, cocoa and butter until it’s thick. Once cooled, the mixture is rolled into bite-size balls. A Brazilian birthday party isn’t complete without a tray of brigadeiros, but they also show up at weddings, baby showers and holiday gatherings. Some cooks skip the rolling altogether and eat the soft mixture with a spoon, a style called brigadeiro de colher.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Sources indicate that in a small saucepan, combine the sweetened condensed milk, cocoa powder and butter. Cook, stirring constantly, on medium-low heat until the mixture is thickened, 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer the mixture to a medium bowl. Refrigerate it, covered, for two hours or until it’s firm enough to be rolled.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Shape the chilled mixture into 1-inch balls. Roll the balls in chocolate sprinkles.

Editor’s Tip: Rub a little butter on your palms before rolling, and grease them again every few balls. This will keep the mixture from sticking and give each truffle a smooth surface.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a recent development, keep brigadeiros in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Store them in paper candy cups or in a single layer separated by parchment so they don’t stick together. Cold brigadeiros get firm, so let them sit out for about 15 minutes before serving to bring back their soft, fudgy centers.

Brigadeiros last up to one week in an airtight container in the refrigerator. They taste best within the first few days while the sprinkles are still crisp.

Yes, you can make brigadeiros ahead of time. Cook the chocolate mixture up to two days in advance and keep it covered in the refrigerator, then roll and coat the truffles the day you blueprint to serve them. If the mixture is too stiff to scoop, let it stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that yes, brigadeiros freeze well. Arrange the rolled truffles on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them until they’re firm, about one hour, then transfer them to an airtight container and freeze them for up to three months. Thaw them overnight in the refrigerator.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

When the brigadeiro mixture stays soft and sticky even after chilling, it almost always means that it needs more time on the stove. Scrape it back into the saucepan and cook it over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for a few more minutes until it thickens and pulls away from the bottom of the pan in one mass. Watch the mixture closely because overcooking will turn it stiff and grainy.

Sources indicate that no, brigadeiros won’t work with regular milk. Brigadeiros depend on the concentrated sugar and milk solids in sweetened condensed milk to cook down into a thick fudge that can be rolled. If you’re out of it, you can make your own sweetened condensed milk by simmering whole milk and sugar until the mixture reduces by about half.

Sources indicate that with my sincerest apologies to Vogue staffers’ favorite pairs of eating pants, when it comes to Thanksgiving fashion, nothing beats the fresh-off-the-runway and fabulous pieces found in Gossip Girl’s now-legendary Thanksgiving episodes. When there’s a svelte Fendi suit or a tapestry McQueen dress on hand, who needs a forgiving drawstring waistband?

Sources indicate that nearly twenty years after the show’s debut, the finer details of those episodes’ familial dramas may be a little murky in memory, but nothing remains as crystal clear as Blair Waldorf’s sharply-defined, uptown girl style. See, for example, the sparkly fall 2007 Marc by Marc Jacobs babydoll dress she dons in season one (episode nine, “Blair Waldorf Must Pie!”). “It’s a defining look for both the character and the show, and I have spent the better part of two decades trying to duplicate it,” says People Like You author and Gossip Girl fashion expert Tyler McCall. “And if you don’t believe that it’s iconic, try and find that dress on the secondhand market for anything close to a reasonable price.”.

Industry observers note that blair Waldorf-approved Marc by Marc Jacobs dresses may not have quite reached the CBK-Calvin Klein craze, but do a cursory search, and that particular babydoll dress is still incredibly difficult to procure. But when paired with a knit capelet, bow-printed tights, and a dainty pair of pumps—as it was in the episode—Miss Waldorf’s holiday style could be easily mistaken for the secondhand wishlist of many fashion girls today.

Season 6: Fendi suit, Gucci blouse, Chloé overcoat.

Another treasured Thanksgiving look of Blair’s includes season two’s backless green dress from the now-shuttered label Alexandra Vidal, topped off by a blue Sretsis dress (worn as a coat!) and some seriously autumnal Jimmy Choo boots. However, when it comes to rivaling the babydoll dress, it’s season three’s Nanette Lepore belted tweed coat, worn over a brown printed Sariah dress, and—once again—statement tights that handily take second place. Today, thanks to Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel, not-your-mother’s tweed is all the rage.

Recent findings suggest that while vintage fashion has had us all in a chokehold for quite some time now, and the runways today resemble twenty years ago more than they did ten, McCall also points out how these looks are in lind with certain trends today, including statement tights ,which have re-entered the fashion conversation. (See from the spring 2027 collections: Jil Sander, Marc Jacobs, Lii, and more.) “Festive tights were a Gossip Girl signature, and that’s a trend that’s stuck around for a few winters now, whether it’s a patterned style or a monochromatic moment,” she states. But still, if you’re looking for something a little less uptown, she recommends channeling one of Serena van der Woodsen’s many silky jewel-toned frocks and tapping into the “lingerie-as-daywear” redux. Somehow, Gossip Girl’s Thanksgiving episodes are a time capsule that captures how all great fashion eventually comes back around.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

It has been revealed that more difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

Latest in this update: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

According to recent reports, food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

Recent findings suggest that there are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

According to recent reports, the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

Industry observers note that what we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

According to recent reports, what we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. 5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

In a recent development, once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

If crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

If steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

Recent findings suggest that the same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

In a recent development, with five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That stated, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

Recent findings suggest that high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

In a recent development, not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

According to recent reports, drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

Recent findings suggest that famed film director Francis Ford Coppola isn’t just known for his Oscar-winning movies—he’s also a prolific winemaker. He sold his namesake winery to Delicato Family Wines in 2021, but the lineup is still just as strong as it was under his leadership.

Tech Report: There’s an Actual Holiday for Eating Thanksgiving Leftovers Over the Kitchen Sink

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.
  • It has been revealed that it’s the morning after Thanksgiving.
  • As it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.

It has been revealed that it’s the morning after Thanksgiving. The good dishes are still drying, the fridge is a Tetris board of foil-wrapped leftovers and you’re standing over the kitchen sink eating cold stuffing with your bare hands. No plate, no judgment.

As it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience. It’s called Sinkie Day, and it’s been around since long before TikTok made girl dinner a thing.

Industry observers note that for that, we have Norm Hankoff to thank. An advertising consultant from California, he had his lightbulb moment in 1991 “while wolfing down some tuna salad over his sink, using extra-strength potato chips as utensils,” according to a 1997 Associated Press report.

Recent findings suggest that convinced he couldn’t be the only one, Hankoff founded the International Association of People Who Dine Over the Kitchen Sink and declared the day after Thanksgiving Sinkie Day. By 1997, more than 1,000 people had joined, and each one received a membership certificate stamped with a double sink and the group’s motto: “Everybody does it. Sinkies proudly admit it.”.

It has been revealed that naturally, there was a cookbook—or rather, a don’t-cook book. Published by a organization cheekily called Digester’s Reader, The Official Sinkies Don’t Cook Book included such culinary masterpieces as “cakeless frosting” and “meat loaf in your fist.” Other recipes called for little more than a handful of mashed potatoes or a piece of chocolate cake dunked in a glass of milk.

Recent findings suggest that hankoff even set his sights on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. When Hillary Clinton was looking for a chef in 1994, he sent her a copy of his book and suggested the first family give sink-side snacking a try. No word on whether they took his advice, but the White House did send him a thank-you letter.

Sources indicate that the beauty of Sinkie Day, which falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, is that it’s perhaps the only food holiday that actively encourages you to do less. A fridge full of Thanksgiving extras is all it takes, though a few upgrades never hurt:.

It has been revealed that of course, a holiday devoted to leftovers is also a good excuse to brush up on food safety. As long as everything hit the fridge within two hours of cooking, you’ve got three to four days to work your way through it.

Are you a proud Sinkie? Let us know in the comments below!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every guy needs the best beard trimmer for his situation. Whether he grows it patchy, keeps it perma-stubbled, or is as lustrous as the A-List beards, a trimmer is mandatory in every beard kit. And not all beard trimmers are alike, which is why the best one for your facial hair style may be different from the next guy’s.

Recent findings suggest that I tested a bunch of beard trimmers to deliver you a real who’s who of men’s grooming devices. This list reflects a range of options—some multitaskers, some detailers; some top-shelf, some a better buy for lower budgets. Above all, though, I ask you this: Make sure that the device you choose allows your beard to reach its full potential. That doesn’t mean you need a big bushy beard, but rather, you should be able to achieve whichever style (or a suite of styles) you want to wear over the next few years—which is the minimum amount of time any of these devices should last. Ideally, they’ll hum on for five to 10 years, anyhow.

Industry observers note that here are the best beard trimmers after we tested pretty much every last one of them. (And while you’re at it, consider my rosters of other grooming tools, from razors and electric shavers, to manscapers and hair clippers.).

No sense in burying the headline: Philips Norelco’s Multigroom 9000 Series is, hands down, the best beard trimmer you can buy. And that’s before factoring in how much more it can do than just keep your facial hair in check than other electric razors that are found in your everyday grooming kit. (It’s also recently been renamed the “All-in-One 9000” but answers to both names.) For the last 5 or 6 years, this has been my single go-to trimmer. Everything else is trying to dethrone it, and so far, no true contest has emerged. In terms of customization and power, this device checks all of the boxes.

In a recent development, it all starts with the beating heart: "The Multigroom does not compromise on power or battery life, and it's very intuitive to use," indicates Fellow Barber’s Head of Education Emily Clark. The battery life truly over-delivers: your mileage may vary since Philips Norelco only claims a (still impressive) six hours of charge, but I got a ridiculous 17 hours of consecutive runtime fresh out of the box, thanks to a lithium ion battery. Speaking of the box, there’s a lot in there, all of it useful. Between the small tooth-like detail attachment and foil shaving head, the Multigroom 9000 makes it easy to style and sculpt with precision. One trimmer even adjusts by tenths of a millimeter to help you get the perfect designer stubble, if that's your aim. And that’s just its beard trimming bona fides. The Multigroom 9000 is also a solid hair trimmer (shout out to that brawny motor and battery again) and body hair trimmer as well. Covering off for three products, and doing it well, suddenly makes the $90 price tag look like a deal.

Recent findings suggest that long-term testing notes: Wouldn’t you know it… I lost the beloved little shaver on this one recently. Heartbreak. (Yeah, I can test a upcoming one, but I realize now how much of my love for it is pinned on that micro shaving attachment.) I stand by the fact that it’s the best on the market, but without that shaver, the window has opened for me to spend time with other devices, like the Braun below. Let this be a lesson: Don’t unpack your Philips Norelco all-in-one in a hotel room without carefully auditing every single piece when you pack it up again. Adam Hurly.

What Amazon Reviewers Are Saying.

Recent findings suggest that "This trimmer is great! It comes with so many attachments to use for your trimming needs. The battery lasts a long time, i have yet to have to charge mine and i've had it for a few months now.

The trimmer is super quiet as well as very well made. It's all made up of metal, not plastic, and feels like it will last a long time. It's fairly lightweight and easy to handle when [using] it. It also comes with a small cleaning brush that makes cleaning it up a breeze!".

According to recent reports, given how much I love the Philips Norelco Multigroom 9000, it’s no surprise that the more affordable model, the Multigroom 5000, is my budget choice to keep things manscaped. It offers most of the same steel-bladed precision and customization benefits as its fancier family member, albeit in a less durable body (plastic instead of stainless steel) and half the battery life. Still, its a three-hour battery power beast that bests many beard trimmers twice the price. And the lighter plastic body is nice for travel. The Philips Norelco Multigroom 5000 is great for anyone on a budget, but it’s not “budget.".

According to recent reports, whereas other lower-priced beard trimmers can’t handle precise detailing, the Multigroom 5000 includes a detail trimmer and nose trimmer, not to mention hair clipper and body trimmer guards for versatility. It does lack the shaving detailer and the body shaver (as does the in-between 7000 model), which is vital to note if you want that level of customization and don’t otherwise own a detail shaver that you also rely upon for bare-faced stretches of facial real estate. For this reason, I find it a little less perfect across the board compared to the 9000, but the price-to-precision ratio is hard to match. And if you want a great value above all—and a straightforward beard trimmer—meet your optimal Multigroom, the 5000.

Long-term testing notes: Recently, I used the 5000 consistently, and got quite cozy with it. Sure, it lacked the key shaving features of the 9000, but I think this is truly the best value device in the game when you only want a trimmer. Terrific muscle, terrific customization, great endurance. Five stars for this one. Adam Hurly.

What Amazon Reviewers Are Saying.

According to recent reports, "This Phillips/Norelco trimmer works great. It is very quiet, the battery life is pretty long and it does exactly what I need it to do. It has been revealed that hatteker is a surprise of a buy—it’s that “out of left field” Amazon brand that most of us recognize by name, despite not knowing anyone who uses it. Industry observers note that long-term testing notes: Every time I bring this one out, I am amused by how surprisingly great it is. Adam Hurly.

If you’re researching beard trimmers, you’ll see the term “zero-gap” a lot. So, what’s a zero-gap trimmer? A zero-gap trimmer cuts as close to the skin as possible, effectively a 0mm cutting length. Industry observers note that you want a beard trimmer that’s simple, effective, and doesn’t come with useless features or add-ons. Here are a few features to consider when looking for a great beard trimmer.

We look at how evenly a trimmer cuts, how comfortable it is to use, and whether its attachments make different jobs easier. Power matters, but so do the small frustrations that become obvious with regular use – awkward combs, difficult cleanup, or a handle that’s hard to hold. We also compare battery life, charging, and the range of cutting lengths against the price.

In a recent development, adam Hurly has reviewed grooming products since 2013, and his years of testing underpin this guide. Timothy Beck Werth contributes his own hands-on findings alongside his wider coverage of grooming and consumer technology. What is the best beard trimmer?

There’s no denying: The Philips Norelco Multigroom 9000 is the best beard trimmer you can buy these days. If its $100 price tag is too steep, the baby-brother Multigroom 5000 is a solid fallback. It’s not shower-proof, has a shorter warranty (five years to the 9000’s eight years), has a plastic body instead of steel, and comes with a few less attachments. But at $40, it gets the basics done nearly as well as it’s pricier sibling.

Can you use a beard trimmer to cut head hair?

Industry observers note that beard trimmers are not meant to be used as hair clippers, since clippers require much more power to cut through thicker patches of hair. However, some beard trimmers have the muscle to multitask, and they’ll proudly hype that skill—usually by declaring the work for “beard and head” or similar language. We usually verify those claims against product reviews, too. And frankly, we’d probably just opt to buy a dedicated hair trimmer (you can find our roundup of the best hair trimmers here), especially if you’ll be using it often.

Which beard trimmer do barbers use?

Recent findings suggest that barbers choose tools to suit the job, from adjustable trimmers for controlling length, to detail trimmers for sharper edges. The Wahl Pro Series High Visibility is our professional pick for precision work, while the Philips Norelco Multigroom range offers broader versatility. For home use, start with your beard length and the kind of maintenance you do most often – a tool built for crisp outlines won’t necessarily include the guards you need to trim a longer beard evenly.

Which trimmer number is best for a beard?

That's going to depend on what beard style you're going with. In order to play around with trimmer numbers, we like the Braun All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 9440 for its easy-to-use adjustment wheel.

How do you use a beard trimmer?

It has been revealed that first, wash and dry your beard so you're starting off with a clean canvas. Then, decide how short or long you want to keep that bad boy. Trim against the grain of your growth, and know that the direction of growth may vary even in similar locations on the face. It's OK to make a couple of passes to ensure you get each hair because a patchy beard is a bad beard. Finally, clean up the neckline with some sharp lines so it's neat and tidy, framing the perfection that is your beautiful facial hair.

How do I maintain and clean a beard trimmer?

Switch it off and disconnect the charger before cleaning, then remove trapped hair from the blades and combs after each use. Follow the instructions for your particular model – a washable cutting head doesn’t mean the whole handle can go under the tap. The Remington Vacuum trimmer, for example, has removable washable parts, but its body should stay out of water.

It has been revealed that let washed components dry before putting them away. Oil the blades if the manufacturer tells you to, but don’t assume every trimmer needs it. Philips’ current Multigroom blades are designed to work without oiling. Replace a damaged or persistently blunt cutting unit with the correct part for your model.

How do I choose the right trimmer if I have sensitive skin or ingrown hairs?

It has been revealed that avoid “zero-gap” trimmers, which is a trimmer that cuts as close to the skin as possible, effectively a 0mm cutting length—those can mess your skin if you're prone to irritation or ingrowns. Otherwise, since you're trimming, you usually won't have to worry about irritating your skin because the blades shouldn't ever actually make contact with your face.

What’s the best way to travel with a beard trimmer—any TSA or voltage concerns?

One of the big concerns for frequent travelers—at least in the USA—is whether they're going to be able to get their beard trimmer through security and not having it buzz during transport. If this is a priority for you, look for a model with a travel lock like the Braun All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 9440, which prevents the trimmer from turning on in transit.

How do I clean a waterproof vs. non-waterproof trimmer?

In a recent development, waterproof trimmers are a breeze: Just hit ‘em with the (usually included) cleaning brush, then wash them off in the sink before drying and applying some oil. Non-waterproof trimmers just skip the rinse, so you’ll have to take extra care with the brush. You can also use spray cleaners specifically designed for grooming electricals depending on your trimmer's care instructions.

What should I do if my trimmer starts pulling hair or losing power?

First, make sure you've thoroughly cleaned the trimmer. Next, make sure it's fully charged and/or has fresh batteries. If it's still pulling hair, it's probably time to swap the blades (plenty of companies sell refills on their site, and make sure to check the warranty to see if you qualify for a fresh set). If it's losing power, it might be time to swap the internal battery (check your warranty!) or get a new trimmer altogether. Luckily, we haven't had that matter with any of the trimmers listed above.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

Where others zig, Whitney Peak zags.

The actor, who just wrapped the lengthy press tour for her new film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, easily could have indulged in a method dressing spree (and many of her castmates did!). But it was Peak’s restraint that earned her a spot on Vogue’s 2026 Best Dressed list. “It’s my first time doing a press tour of this scale, and with all nerves and excitement, I just wanted to feel like myself in whatever I was wearing,” the actor tells Vogue.

Sources indicate that “We talked about [method dressing], but ultimately decided not to,” she claims of working with stylist Karla Welch. “I think the fun was in watching fans find their own connections between my character and what I was wearing.” Instead, Peak and Welch were guided by instinct. “I had a very general Pinterest board that I shared with Karla: images, textures, shapes I loved. But honestly, we worked very intuitively with each other and established a real flow,” she says. “The looks reflected that—they feel connected, have a rhythm, and they feel authentic.”.

Sources indicate that though she wore Chanel aplenty (“I had too much fun in that dress,” she indicates of her black multi-patterned look in Berlin), brands of all size were on the table. Peak was particularly enamored with the quilted floral silk jacquard Dries Van Noten coat she paired with a suit and tie (“THAT COAT! Everything.”) and the cutout Torishéju she trotted out in New York (“I’d never worn anything like it.”).

In a recent development, and, although she swore off method dressing, Peak did end with an overt nod to her character, Lenore Dove Baird, in a blue velvet Robert Wun, a white dove pulling at her suspended shoulder strap. “The Robert Wun was the perfect, magical ending,” she says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

Sources indicate that it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

According to recent reports, while this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

In a recent development, but getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

It has been revealed that this is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an key role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous Fresh York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

Ellie Martin Cliffe For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that according to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

Moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He says that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

Industry observers note that for gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

It has been revealed that this is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

And if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

Recent findings suggest that PSA: This vegan pumpkin pie is so good, it might rival the classic. It’s just as easy as any other pumpkin pie recipe, if not easier. Bonus points: the nutty, pecan-based crust is naturally gluten-free! Using coconut oil in the crust and coconut milk in the filling, I was able to replicate the richness of pumpkin pie without sacrificing any flavor. This vegan treat will satisfy those pumpkin pie cravings, but with a unique nutty crust that amplifies all the fall flavors.

What People Are Saying:“This is my family's FAVORITE vegan pumpkin pie - we make it every year…” - GoldPaw.

It has been revealed that the best part about this pie is that you don’t need to chill the pie dough at all. Preheat your oven to 375° and grease your pie plate.

Then, use a food processor to pulse the pecans, oats, sugar, and salt until they’re fine crumbs. Stream in the coconut oil and then pulse until the dough forms. You’re done! The easiest pie dough you’ll ever make.

Press the dough into your greased pie plate in an even layer– make sure you press the dough up the sides of the pan as well. Place parchment over the dough and fill with dried beans, rice, or pie weights. Bake for 10 minutes and then remove the parchment and bake for another 10 minutes.

To make the filling, whisk all of the filling ingredients together in a large bowl. Pour it into the par-baked crust, smoothing the top.

Bake the pie in the oven for 50 to 55 minutes. If the crust starts to get too dark, cover the whole pie with foil. You’ll know the pie is done when it looks set and dry on top but is still slightly jiggly in the center. Let cool in the refrigerator before serving with some whipped topping alongside.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Keep your pie in the fridge for up to 4 days, loosely covered with foil. Keep the whipped cream separate and dollop onto each pie slice as you serve. If the whipped cream loses structure, keep it cold and re-whip with a handheld mixer as needed.

The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

Culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the tech giant is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

According to recent reports, the biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

In a recent development, this is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

According to recent reports, whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Recent findings suggest that lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

In a recent development, transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

As much as I love a substantial, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

According to recent reports, I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

One of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

Industry observers note that start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that this trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

Sources indicate that I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.
