“This Star System Should Not Exist”: Astronomers Discover a Cosmic Mystery Just 28 Light-Years Away

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.
  • In a recent development, A planet too faint to see can still give itself away by making the star it orbits wobble.
  • According to recent reports, “We were actually looking for planets,” said lead author Étienne Artigau, a researcher at Université de Montréal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.

In a recent development, A planet too faint to see can still give itself away by making the star it orbits wobble. Astronomers looking for planets around a dim red star 28 light-years from Earth measured a wobble more than a thousand times larger than they expected. Following that motion revealed a family of three stars, two of which had already run out of fuel.

According to recent reports, “We were actually looking for planets,” said lead author Étienne Artigau, a researcher at Université de Montréal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx). “Instead, we found something much more surprising.”.

The star they were watching was a red dwarf, a star much dimmer than the Sun. At the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi, a planet-hunting instrument called SPIRou (SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge) picked up a change of nearly 16 kilometers (10 miles) per second in the star’s speed. After several years of follow-up observations, the team knew that whatever was tugging on the red dwarf had more than half the Sun’s mass.

“The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star,” stated Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and co-author of the study. “The most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldn’t be ruled out.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team finally saw the faint companion with Gemini North, another telescope on Maunakea. High-resolution images from its ʻAlopeke instrument showed a white dwarf orbiting the red dwarf. A white dwarf is the extremely dense core a star leaves behind after it runs out of fuel. Most stars, including the Sun, will end their lives this way.

In a recent development, astronomers already knew about a white dwarf much farther out. That outer star circles both the red dwarf and its newly spotted companion. No other trio like this one, named Welopōʻai, is known within 100 light-years of Earth.

Before it became a white dwarf, the red dwarf’s closer neighbor was about 40 percent more massive than the Sun. As it aged, it swelled into a giant several hundred times its original size. The red dwarf would have been close enough for the expanding giant to affect it. In similar systems, a giant can swallow its companion, and the two stars can even merge. Welopōʻai’s red dwarf appears to have survived. It now circles the remnant in a stable orbit, farther away than astronomers would expect given how close the two once were.

It has been revealed that “This system should not exist,” mentioned Patrick Dufour, a professor at Université de Montréal who studies white dwarfs and co-authored the paper. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”.

Sources indicate that the team wants to find out whether the pull of all three stars on one another could explain the inner pair’s orbit. The researchers also measured the inner white dwarf’s mass with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent. Astronomers rarely get such a precise mass for a white dwarf, and it gives them a way to test predictions about how stars age and how matter behaves when packed so tightly together. The international team, led by IREx, reported its in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Industry observers note that the simulation illustrates how gravitational interactions between its three stars could influence their orbits over time. The sonification translates the stars’ orbital motions into sound, so you can hear the system’s changing rhythms. Credit: Heidi White (UMONTREAL/IREx). Simulation data: Alexandre Correia, University of Coimbra.

Industry observers note that welopōʻai got its name through A Hua He Inoa (“To Call Forth a Name”), a program of the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The name joins welo, an inherited or family trait, with pōʻai, an orbit or circular path. Together they evoke a “path of family traits.”.

“Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” Artigau said. “Even when we’re searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us.”.

Sources indicate that reference: “Welopō‘ai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun” by Étienne Artigau, Charles-Antoine Parent, Atanas K. Stefanov, Érika Le Bourdais, Souleymane Ouedraogo, Alexandrine L’Heureux, Patrick Dufour, René Doyon, Neil J. Cook, Charles Cadieux, Clémence Fontanive, Luc Arnold, Jean-François Donati, Matthias R. Schreiber, Ryan Cloutier, Xavier Delfosse, Céline Reylé, Thierry Forveille, Tianqi Cang, Claire Moutou and Alexandre C. M. Correia, 19 November 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics.   • Recent findings suggest that if a organization funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected one million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground.. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. And according to a new paper, available in preprint on arXiv by Federico Toson, a researcher at the University of Padova in Italy, the math that regulatory agencies use to determine whether a satellite is âsafeâ in these highly congested spaces is fundamentally flawed.

To understand why, letâs look at how engineers at the moment grade collision risk. Standards set by NASA and the European Space Agency rely on color-coded charts that sort missions into one of several buckets based on their risk profile. Categories like âLow,â âMedium,â and âHighâ are self-explanatory, but they eliminate notable distinctions in risk profiles, and only look at one satellite at a time. And, crucially, they focus solely on the risk to the company that rolled out them.

Recent findings suggest that if a organization funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company. But if a mega-constellation operator builds thousands of identical satellites at a cost of a million dollars a pop, losing one barely registers on their financial statements. Consequently, according to the risk profile, all relatively inexpensive, reproducible satellites that make up the mega-constellations end up with a âLowâ risk profile.

Fraser talks about how we make sure satellites don't crash into each other.

It has been revealed that the algorithm described in the paper exposes the flaw in that logic by separating the risk into two different scores. First is the âIndividual Riskâ â i.e. the traditional metric of the financial hit a satelliteâs owner takes if the spacecraft is destroyed by collision. The second is the âCollective Riskâ, which ignores the cost of each individual satellite, but captures the physical danger each imposes on every other operational satellite in its altitude band across its entire operational and disposal lifetime.

According to recent reports, mathematically, this is a way of capturing the âtragedy of the commonsâ aspect of orbital space. Economists have long warned that when a âpublic goodâ (such as an orbital path) is free to use, people, whether they are farmers on a field or launch companies trying to build internet satellite constellations, have an incentive to utilize as much of the free resource as they can while not paying any attention to the consequences of that use.

Industry observers note that in orbit, those consequences take the form of congestion, dodging maneuvers, and potential destruction of other satellites that are forced on every other manufacturer if one decides to ignore their responsibility to properly manage the impact their equipment has on an orbit. As weâve reported before, those consequences are growing, with an average Starlink satellite having to fire its thruster at least once a week to dodge a potential collision.

Fraser talks about how space junk could eventually block our access to orbit.

In a recent development, starlink itself is a good case in point. A single Starlink V2 Mini, orbiting at 525 km, has a collective risk 317 times higher than the âindividual risk.â In a traditional risk assessment, this would mark it as âLowâ risk, whereas this upcoming framework would place it very clearly in the âVery Highâ camp.

Sources indicate that there have been some efforts to capture this long-term environmental impact already. ESA uses an index called the Environmental Consequences of Orbital Breakups (ECOB) and researchers at EPFL in Switzerland have put forward the Space Sustainability Rating. However, the simulations underpinning these metrics are computationally expensive and require hours to complete. The tool Toson developed in MATLAB runs in seconds on a standard computer and matches the higher-end benchmarks exceptionally well.

Itâs all good to simply patch the categorization of a satellite for its collective risk, but having that information is useless if operators and regulators donât do anything with it. Toson suggests updating the international debris guidelines and licensing rules to take this new metric into account. If a firm wants to launch a low-cost satellite that will affect the orbital environment for everyone else, they should be required to either fund active debris cleanup or accept a cap on the total risk posed by their fleet of spacecraft.

Fraser talks about real-life advanced tech that can remove space debris.

Regulators havenât had much time to digest this new idea, so donât expect to see any such rules anytime soon. But as our orbital highways become more and more congested, satellite operators will need more guidance on how to maintain the commons before we end up in a Kessler Syndrome situation. This new paper may contribute to that standards-setting â and the sooner the better.

Industry observers note that forgive the Daddy Warbucks-ness of what I’m about to say, but I think it’s crucial to remember that a splurge and an extravagance aren’t quite the same thing when it comes to gifts. On one end of the spectrum, there are vapid luxury items; on the other, there are the gifts whose steeper price point is tied directly to their artistry, quality, and/or durability. While the former can be fun to window-shop, our hard-earned clams are best spent on the latter.

As a seasoned shopping writer, I ask myself two major questions when mulling over a pricey purchase: What is the story behind this item? Can I picture it in my life for years to come?

Consider the iconic, mid-century modern Moccamaster coffee machine, which first debuted in the 1960s and has been trending on social media lately for its array of colorful, modular designs. I took the cult-fave machine for an extended test run (it’s still my daily driver), and the yellow pepper iteration made me fall in love with drip coffee all over again. The Dutch manufacturer behind the appliance, Technivorm, really exercises what it calls its core tenets of “form and function,” and will service any repairs on the machines for up to five years. That is exactly the kind of lore I crave from the splurge-level items on my holiday shopping list (and the kind that will make your own design-savvy, coffee-loving giftee feel special).

If you’re reaching into your budget for gifts that last, impress, and — if you’re giving them to a family member or partner — you might be able to use yourself for years to come, the fancy gifts for food lovers start getting good. There are the major-ticket kitchen titans: a high-tech Mill food recycler, sleek Miele vacuums (post-kitchen-prep cleanup doesn’t stand a chance), and electric pizza ovens that can reach 850 degrees Fahrenheit in just 90 seconds. Sometimes “splurges” are just wise investments, especially with appliances and cookware; your giftee is going to use a well-made cutting board or top-tier kitchen knife for years or decades to come. There are also the gifts with spectacular whimsy: a stationary exercise bike that makes smoothies, a martini-lover’s menorah, a tabletop lighter that’s also an incredible conversation piece.

Industry observers note that these gifts may be at higher price points than a classic stocking stuffer, but they’re also extra-special — we’d say, so worth it if you have the dough. If you’re looking to roll out the red carpet with splurge-worthy food and kitchen gifts, look no further.

The casual gift for someone who loves food and loves to host might be nice set of chip and dip bowls, cocktail napkins, or perhaps some beeswax candlesticks. The gift of a whole dry-cured Spanish ham leg, however, is a next-level present for the most passionate entertainer in your family or friend group.

No better way to pull focus at the dining table than with this copper and brass pepper mill, which East Fork says can literally last for “hundreds of years” when cared for properly. The 10-inch tall grinder is made in collaboration with a small, family-run organization in Greece, and is actually modeled after the same mills 20th-century Greek soldiers would carry to grind coffee, a fact that finds homage in the Greek lettering inscribed on the mill.

The Eater staff has tested its fare share of toaster ovens, and crowned the Balmuda as one of the best for its minimalist design and ability to not just warm but rehydrate breads and pastries; it uses a steam process to reinvigorate that day-old croissant like a wizard. This Balmuda Pro has an even more powerful heat source, and a setting called Salamander Grill Mode for giving your salmon the restaurant-grade finishing treatment.

According to recent reports, the cultural martini discourse has never been stronger, or brinier. Help your giftee celebrate Hanukkah with Susan Alexandra’s dirty martini menorah. As the designer’s site proclaims, “The miracle of Hanukkah was that the olive oil that was enough only for one day of light lasted for eight days. Our favorite way of consuming olives? In a bath of vodka/ gin and a touch of vermouth!”.

Behold, a splurge that is also a cooking investment! We’ve all experienced the frustration of chopping special ingredients on a sub-par cutting board, and the moment you level up to a thick, handsome slab is one that can help give you newfound confidence and efficiency as a passionate home cook. Boardsmith’s walnut end grain cutting boards are all made to order out of a sustainably harvested black walnut, resulting in beautiful, checkerboard-like and ombré color variations. Cheese boards have never looked better, folks.

In a recent development, the Chicago-based luxury chocolatier Vosges is known for its intricate, decadent holiday gifts (don’t miss its lodge-inspired advent calendar), and it has curated the perfect assortment of its truffles to go with a bottle of Ceretto Barolo wine. “This is a classic Barolo,” the site explains, “[it’s] light garnet in color with Barolo’s quintessential aromas of roses, tart cherries, and hints of truffles.”.

Made in Victor, Idaho, the boutique blades of Fresh West KniveWorks are a departure from the recent fad of making knives extra wide, favoring instead the graceful docility of a light, 8-inch steel blade and a handle made out of a durable resin composite material that will last a lifetime. In the fighting words of New West, “this precision instrument isn’t a club like Mom’s old Wüsthof Trident.” If you’re shopping for a partner who tends to their knife collection like the Crown Jewels, it’s the kind of gift that feels equal parts lifetime cooking investment and personality-forward essential tool.

Gohar World’s elevated kitchen essentials walk the line between Dalí-esque absurdity (remember when Julia Fox wore its kitchen gloves to the Grammys?) and functionality, and this metallic apron is no exception: it lends you a lacy hand (two, actually) while you’re cooking.

It has been revealed that I really do think the Moccamaster coffee machine is the Platonic ideal of drip coffee machines; my own yellow pepper model swept me off my feet with its talent for quick, smooth brewing and its modular, chic mid-century modern design. If you love someone who loves coffee — and perhaps already owns the GOATed machine — why not invest in the brand’s powerful burr grinder? It’s certified by the European Coffee Brewing Centre (ECBC), which means it has passed a rigorous testing process for uniform grinding and quality construction.

Recent findings suggest that imagine casually inviting your beloved over for dinner, and you serve this gorgeous Japanese wagyu ribeye steak along with an Old-Fashioned? Imperia Caviar is best known for its royal osetra, but it’s also where you can find a variety of A5 Japanese wagyu (the highest designation for beef in the country); this grade of wagyu has up to five times more intramuscular fat, which makes for an even richer, buttery flavor.

In a recent development, I always have a few lighters floating around my house for candles and incense, but there’s something so retro-chic about a coffee table lighter. Edie Parker, master of eccentric and surreal lifestyle [puffs chamomile pre-roll] accessories has a line of jelly-inspired tabletop lighters with all kinds of “fillings,” and the olive version is one of the most charming.

Unsurprisingly, we’re picky when it comes to choosing cookware at Eater — that’s why we collaborated with Heritage Steel to make the kind of cookware collection that will last a lifetime. Every frypan, lid, and pot is made out of 5-ply stainless steel, and this robust bundle includes everything you need to embark on all kinds of culinary adventures: two fry pans (8.5- and 10.5-inch), a 2-quart saucier, a 3-quart saucepan, a 4-quart sauté pan, and an 8-quart stock pot ready to simmer your most Strega Nona-worthy stews.

In a recent development, here’s an idea: Order this massive wheel of Manchego cheese from Flamingo Estate, and ride it to victory at the Cooper’s Hill cheese rolling competition. That, or gift it to someone who can appreciate the fact that it’s sourced, per Flamingo Estate, from one of only ten cheese mongers in Spain that are still making farmstead PDO Manchego Artesano, which results in an even richer and more complex flavor.

You know the massive (or rather, full-size) Rocco: a $1,500 high-tech drink fridge, endorsed by Eric Wareheim and seemingly designed by someone who loves Eames chairs. This year, Rocco has launched a miniature version of its posh drink refrigerator, dubbed the Mini Mini Fridge, this 14-inch tall personal fridge fits up to 12 cans of your preferred beverages (or sheet masks; choose your journey). Unlike most mini fridges, the Mini cools down to 39 degrees Fahrenheit (the majority of countertop fridges hit 48 degrees Fahrenheit at their coldest). Kind of the dream set up for your — sorry, your giftee’s — office.

Atelier Sebastião Lobo crafts otherworldly flatware that’s almost too beautiful to use. This set of Calder-esque cutlery has spawned many imitations, because it’s one of the most original designs to come out of the flatware world in recent years, and a prime example of how cutlery and tableware in general got really squiggly and freaky this year.

There is nothing like devoting counter space to yet another coffee machine that requires highly specific capsules, but hey! This one is different — it brews only cold coffee. (Nitro cold brew, cold brew, and cold espresso to be specific.) Sure, it’s definitely a bit of a luxury, but then again, so is spending $7 on an iced cortado from the coffee shop every morning.

N/A drinks were created to be a more inclusive product. Only a rare few can order bottles of bubbly for over $100. The Venn diagram where these two groups overlap is small, but it exists, along with this $119 bottle of booze-free bubbly made with French Chardonnay grapes.

In a way that I cannot quite explain, this feels like it’s targeted at the 1990s kids who grew up with Smart House and Richie Rich. This stationary exercise bike, complete with an orange slice wheel, whips up one of your favorite smoothies courtesy of your own pedaling power. As one reviewer writes, “I am 67 years old, widowed twice, and I have seen enough in this life to know when somebody has finally invented something useful. This bicycle-blender contraption has changed the direction of my spirit. Every morning I put in one banana, some frozen peaches, yogurt, a little honey, and whatever green thing is closest to expiration in my refrigerator. Then I pedal until either the smoothie is done or I start seeing little sparkles. Whichever comes first.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM).
  • Industry observers note that this image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation. This display of illuminated gas came into being when a massive star exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. When it exploded, it expelled its outer layers. Those layers slammed into the interstellar medium, and are lit up by the energy from the shock, and that's what we see today.

Industry observers note that astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM). These explosions shape the dynamics in the ISM, including how stars form there. SNRs also reveal a lot about their progenitor stars. For these and other reasons, they're rich astronomical targets.

Industry observers note that this image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy. But that telescope also has a side hustle: capturing stunning images for the rest of us that don't necessarily add anything to scientific understanding.

One of the main efforts to understand dark energy, the puzzling force that drives the expansion of the Universe, is the Dark Energy Survey. It uses a special, purpose-built camera to do its work, called the Dark Energy Camera (DECam.) DECam is a powerful, 570 megapixel, wide-angle camera mounted on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. It used its power to capture this image of the Betta Fish Nebula.

Like many telescopes, DECam sometimes takes a break from its main job and captures images purely for public interest. It's a way for the professional astronomy community to share some celestial wonder with the rest of us. The latest DECam images of the Betta Fish nebula are in that category.

Industry observers note that only part of the nebula actually looks like a Betta, the popular and colourful aquarium fish. They're also known as Siamese Fighting Fish, but whatever name is used, they're popular for their brilliant colours and flowing fins.

This close-up view shows one portion of the Betta Fish Nebula, the part that most closely resembles its namesake. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

What's left of the exploded star is a collapsed, ultra-dense stellar core called a neutron star. It's tiny, only about 20 km across, and is invisible in this image. It's actually a pulsar with unusual properties that has been studied extensively. It's radio-quiet and can only be detected in x-rays, and also lacks a pulsar wind nebula. It's so unusual that some researchers think it may be an example of what's called a 'low-mass bare strange star.'.

It has been revealed that this is a less visually interesting, more scientific x-ray image of the central portion of the Betta Fish nebula. It indicates what's left of the progenitor star that exploded, labelled in the center. Image Credit: Eppens et al. MNRAS 528, 2095â2111 (2024).

But those scientific details take a back seat to the image's visual interest.

These images have been 'dumbed-down' for internet use. There's a version of the image here that lets you zoom-in and explore it in much greater detail.

This zoomed-in image highlights the part of the nebula that gave it its name. A cooperative orange/red star even serves as the Betta Fish's eye. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

DECam has been observing for more than a decade, and over that time its created a nice catalogue of fantastic images. Here's a few of them.

It has been revealed that here are three DECam images the camera has captured over the years purely for public interest. From left to right: the cometary globule CG4, the Rosette Nebula, and the Corona Australis Molecular Cloud. Image Credits: NSF NOIRLab DECam Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The warmth of planets and dead stars is helping scientists narrow the possibilities for dark matter, offering new clues about the mysterious substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Sources indicate that most of the matter in the universe is something scientists have never directly seen. Known as dark matter, it is thought to make up about 85% of all matter, yet its true nature remains a mystery. Researchers know it exists largely because of its gravitational effects, but they still do not know what it is made of.

Scientists have spent decades searching for particles that could explain dark matter, without directly detecting any. One possibility is that some particles move so slowly that they barely register in laboratory experiments. However, those same particles might be easier to find in places much larger than any detector on Earth: planets and stars.

Researchers Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard, and Gaurav Tomar investigated whether these celestial bodies could act as natural traps for dark matter. Their study, published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP), found no evidence of dark matter but helped rule out certain possibilities about its properties.

Dark matter is known to interact through gravity, but scientists suspect it may also have extremely weak electrical or magnetic properties. Some particles could carry a tiny electric charge or behave like miniature magnets, allowing them to interact with ordinary matter in ways that are difficult to detect.

Sources indicate that speed could make those interactions even harder to observe. When a slow-moving particle strikes material inside a detector, it may transfer too little energy to produce a measurable signal. Inside a planet or star, however, even a small loss of energy could be enough to prevent the particle from escaping the object’s gravitational pull.

Industry observers note that over billions of years, these trapped particles could accumulate near the center of a planet or star. If their properties allow it, they might eventually collide and undergo a process called annihilation, transforming into other particles. Some of the resulting particles could escape into space, while others could release energy that warms the surrounding material.

In a recent development, “In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” explains Gaurav Tomar, a researcher at the Center for Quantum Spacetime at Sogang University in South Korea and the study’s corresponding author. “There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers used two different approaches to look for signs of dark matter. For Earth and the Sun, they examined existing searches for neutrinos, tiny particles that can travel through enormous amounts of matter without being stopped. If dark matter particles were annihilating deep inside these bodies, some of the resulting neutrinos might reach detectors and provide evidence of what was happening.

For Jupiter and white dwarfs, which are dense remnants of stars, the team looked at heat instead. Unlike the Sun, these objects are not powered by ongoing nuclear fusion, making them potentially useful places to investigate whether another source of energy is contributing to their warmth.

Sources indicate that the researchers calculated how much heat different types of dark matter could produce if captured inside these objects, then compared those predictions with the energy the objects actually emit. If a particular type of dark matter would generate more heat than an object releases, that scenario could be ruled out.

By combining these calculations with existing observations, the team excluded several combinations of dark matter particle mass and electromagnetic properties that previous experiments had not eliminated. Earth was particularly useful for investigating particles with extremely small electric charges, while white dwarfs helped constrain other possible electromagnetic interactions.

The findings also come with an notable uncertainty. How much dark matter a celestial body could capture depends partly on how much dark matter surrounds it. For white dwarfs in particular, researchers must rely on estimates because the local dark matter density is not always known.

It has been revealed that “We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar notes.

It has been revealed that he was referring to the M4 star cluster, where the white dwarfs examined in the study are located. The amount of dark matter in that region has not been directly measured and must instead be estimated using models.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, Tomar suggests searching for even colder white dwarfs in regions thought to contain more dark matter. Because these stars emit relatively little heat, any additional warming from trapped particles could be easier to identify. Planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system could also offer new opportunities to investigate whether dark matter is quietly accumulating inside celestial bodies.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Celestial probes of dark matter electromagnetic interactions” by Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard and Gaurav Tomar, August 27, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2608.27957.

Tech Report: The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today.
  • It has been revealed that on top of all that, there are plans to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars.
  • It has been revealed that this is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today. Beyond NASA and China's intends to send crewed missions to the Moon by the end of the decade and create permanent infrastructure there, both space agencies hope to put boots on the surface of Mars by the 2030s or 40s. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency (ESA) is active in the Artemis Program and plans to send the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover to the Red Planet in 2028. India aims to send the first "gaganauts" to space next year (as part of its Gaganyaan program).

It has been revealed that on top of all that, there are plans to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars. All of this begs the question of how humans intend to live in extraterrestrial environments and among the stars. What is needed to ensure that humans can not only survive the hazards of being off-world, but also flourish? As Mars City Design CEO Vera Mulyani would say, "How can we thrive, and not just survive?".

It has been revealed that this is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences. In addition to questions related to engineering and astronaut health and safety, astrosociology takes a more holistic outlook and examines the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of humans related to outer space. Consider Abraham Maslow's "Hierarchy of Needs," which begins with the basics (physiological and security needs) and extends upwards to include the immaterial, such as love, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

This challenge motivated Dr. Jim Pass to found the Astrosociology Research Institute (ARI) in 2008, a California-based nonprofit educational organization dedicated to developing astrosociology as a multidisciplinary academic field. As Pass describes on the organization's website, astrosociology is both a subdiscipline of sociology and a multidisciplinary field that includes (but is not limited to) "psychology, anthropology, economics, social psychology, political science, space history, space law, space policy, philosophy, as well as the arts.".

At its core, the ARI's mission comes down to a simple but highly relevant question: "How can social and behavioral scientists collaborate with physical and natural scientists to further the success of space exploration and settlement in the future?" In their latest newsletter, titled "Analog Space Missions: The Astrosociological Factors That Affect Analog Space Missions - Part 1," Pass and his colleagues share the perspectives of analog astronauts who participated in their call for papers and expert commentary by educators, space medics, and systems engineers.

As Mia Belle Parkinson, a postdoctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and ARI's editor-in-chief, wrote in the issue:.

Recent findings suggest that when we talk about preparing for space exploration and settlement, we too often default to the technical: propulsion systems, life support, radiation shielding. These things matter enormously. But so do the quieter, harder-to-quantify questions â how do people build trust in isolated environments? How do cultural backgrounds shape group dynamics? What does it mean, psychologically and socially, to live on the edge of the unknown?

According to recent reports, while analog astronaut training may seem like a relatively fresh idea, it's actually part of a long-standing tradition almost as old as the "Space Race" itself. Before astronauts landed on the Moon, NASA conducted a series of training missions known as the "Apollo Geology Field Trips" between 1964 and 1972. The first field trip saw the first two astronaut groups travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, for a two-day mission to Meteor Crater and other locations that resembled volcanic features on the Moon.

Other locations included the Grand Canyon, the volcanic fields in Hawaii, the Nevada National Security Site, and mountain formations in the Sonoran Desert, New Mexico, Oregon, Alaska, west Texas, and Sudbury, Ontario. Additionally, the Soviets conducted the BIOS-3 experiment within the closed ecosystem built at the Institute of Biophysics in Krasnoyarsk in 1965. This was followed by Tektite I and II in 1969 and 1971, which studied human behavior in a confined, isolated, pressurized habitat on the ocean floor near the U.S. Virgin Islands.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Satoshi Furukawa pedals on the upgraded CEVIS system, keeping muscle and bone density levels during spaceflight. (Credit: NASA).

It has been revealed that since that time, research aboard space stations such as Mir, the International Space Station (ISS), and the Chinese Tiangong space station has provided invaluable knowledge about living in space and the effects of microgravity on humans' mental and physical well-being. However, these studies are not directly relevant to proposed missions that will send astronauts to the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. As Parry writes:.

While extremely valuable for zero-gravity spaceflights, living and working at the bottom of a gravity well presents altogether different conditions, including an inability to manufacture drugs or lift heavy objects. Planning for bases and settlements on the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and eventually beyond can only be simulated on the surface of the Earth to humankind's best approximation even in 2026, because gravity matters!

Recent findings suggest that the first analog astronaut (hereafter AA) profiled was former NASA Advisor, science communicator, and space exploration expert Beth Mund. Mund is an especially experienced AA, having participated in the HI-SEAS (Hawai'i Space Exploration Analog and Simulation) program on the summit of Mauna Loa, Hawai'i, the LunAres Research Station, and the Jules Undersea Lodge. The first involved an all-female crew working together during the height of COVID in an uninsulated temporary habitat with minimal privacy and tough conditions.

Industry observers note that the second took place in a converted World War II bunker in Poland located inside an old hangar. The hangar itself was filled with sand to simulate lunar regolith, and steel doors sealed the habitat and its six-person crew inside a rather confined space. At the Jules Undersea Lodge, located in Key Largo off the southern tip of Florida, Mund and her colleagues entered a submerged habitat with no escape hatches, accessible only through a "wet room" portal.

Sources indicate that looking back at these three missions, Mund noticed patterns that transcended any single environment. While each had its own geography and logistics, confinement was the common theme. From her experiences, Mund identified four universal human responses that were consistent throughout. The first, she wrote, was the importance of improvisation:.

In a recent development, no matter how carefully equipment is designed or schedules are drawn, something always fails... each failure forces us to understand the problem and formulate a response to it in the context of very tight resource constraints. And in adapting, we discover more about ourselves than about the broken machines... These small acts of invention prove that ingenuity is not a luxury in confinement. It is a decisive factor in survival.

Photo of analog astronaut Beth Mund sitting outside the HI-SEAS habitat on the summit of Mauna Kea, Hawai'i. Credit: Beth Mund.

In a recent development, the second lesson was the importance of ritual: "At HI-SEAS, our crew naturally gathered each evening for what I came to think of as our 'campfire,' a circle of debriefing, storytelling, and laughter, even in the cold dome with no flame. In Poland, games became our escape valve, a way to puncture the heaviness of the surveys and the claustrophobic walls. Underwater, simply gazing out the porthole together felt like a ceremony. In every analog, the crew instinctively created moments of reconnection that grounded us, even in places designed to isolate.".

The third lesson for Mund was continuity, as she and her colleagues inherited experiments started by crews they never met and which would be handled by future analog crews. "It gave weight to our confinement, transforming it from a private trial into a communal contribution," she said. "That continuity across crew "generations" is perhaps the most powerful sociological insight of analog missions. We are practicing not only how to live together, but how to build across time, leaving work - and maybe even some data/ insights - for crews who serve next.".

Lastly, there was the inevitability of testing. While every mission includes tests of equipment, plants, and methods for living in space, the experience also tests the limits of human endurance, creativity, and cohesion. This, she wrote, is the true essence of analog astronaut training:.

Industry observers note that from Mars-like lava fields to a Polish bunker to the ocean floor, I have learned that analog missions are not about pretending to be astronauts. They are about practicing human endurance in places that strip away comfort and certainty. In that practice, in all the different shapes it takes across environments, facilities, missions, and crews, lies the real preparation for humanity to endure no matter the circumstances.

Sources indicate that mund is merely one of many analog astronauts profiled in the Astrosociological Insights Forum's newsletter. To include as many testimonials and experiences as possible, the concern was released in two parts, incorporating perspectives not only from AAs but also from several experts in the burgeoning field of Astrosociology. More to follow, so stay tuned! In the meantime, check out some other articles we have about organizations committed to analog astronaut training:.

Tech Report: NASA-Funded Study Reveals a Hidden Effect of Space Radiation on the Brain

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh NASA-funded research reveals that cosmic radiation triggers subtle, sex-specific changes in the brain without causing immediate cognitive problems.
  • Industry observers note that cosmic radiation can change the brain’s immune cells in different ways in males and females, even when no obvious problems with memory or behavior appear.
  • Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people from much of the galactic cosmic radiation that fills space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh NASA-funded research reveals that cosmic radiation triggers subtle, sex-specific changes in the brain without causing immediate cognitive problems.

Industry observers note that cosmic radiation can change the brain’s immune cells in different ways in males and females, even when no obvious problems with memory or behavior appear. A new NASA-funded study in mice found distinct molecular responses to simulated space radiation, raising questions about how prolonged exposure could affect astronauts traveling to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people from much of the galactic cosmic radiation that fills space. These highly energetic particles, often described as cosmic “rays,” can damage spacecraft electronics and potentially affect living tissue. Understanding their effects on the brain is a major concern for future missions beyond Earth’s protective magnetic field.

Researchers at the University of Rochester exposed male and female mice to simulated galactic cosmic radiation at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory at Brookhaven National Laboratory. Led by neuroscience graduate student Mark Osabutey, MBChB, the team used single-cell RNA sequencing to examine nearly 16,000 microglia, the brain’s resident immune cells. This technique allowed scientists to investigate how radiation affected gene activity in individual cells.

Industry observers note that the analysis, published in Scientific Reports, identified different molecular responses in males and females. Male microglia indicated changes involving cellular stress adaptation and metabolism, while female microglia exhibited broader reductions in immune signaling pathways. Neither group showed widespread inflammatory activation or detectable radiation-related cognitive or behavioral impairment at the time of testing.

It has been revealed that “Surprisingly, despite clear molecular changes, we found no widespread inflammatory activation or measurable radiation-associated behavioral impairment at the time we examined,” remarked Osabutey. The findings suggest that cellular responses to radiation can occur without immediately producing measurable functional problems, although their longer-term effects remain unknown.

Sources indicate that despite these sex-specific differences, researchers identified one response shared by both groups. Levels of FKBP5, a protein involved in regulating cellular stress responses, increased in the cortex and dentate gyrus of male and female mice. These brain regions contribute to functions including cognition, learning, and memory.

In a recent development, “We now need to understand whether FKBP5 plays a protective or harmful role, and how different radiation exposures and other spaceflight stressors influence long-term brain health,” said Osabutey. “Our findings highlight the importance of considering biological sex when assessing neurological risks during spaceflight and identify potential pathways for developing protective strategies.”.

Sources indicate that university of Rochester Professor of Neuroscience M. Kerry O’Banion, MD, PhD, has investigated the neurological effects of space radiation for more than 15 years. A member of the Del Monte Institute for Neuroscience, O’Banion previously contributed to research indicating that cosmic radiation could accelerate the onset of Alzheimer’s disease.

It has been revealed that “We know cognitive changes from exposure to radiation in space are a real risk,” O’Banion remarked. “It’s vital we understand how brain cells are changed. Knowing which mechanisms are impacted and how may help the development of countermeasures to protect or lessen an astronaut’s exposure to space radiation.”.

The latest findings do not establish whether the observed immune cell changes are harmful, protective, or temporary. Researchers also cannot yet determine whether they contribute to neurological problems after prolonged exposure. “Additional studies examining other time points and effects in other experimental systems will be required to understand this further,” O’Banion said.

In a recent development, osabutey has participated in NASA-funded research since joining O’Banion’s laboratory. In 2023, he received a NASA predoctoral grant augmentation award to investigate changes in microglial populations following exposure to galactic cosmic radiation. He has also presented the laboratory’s research at a NASA conference and attended the European Space Agency Summer School in Darmstadt, Germany.

According to recent reports, “Receiving NASA support has allowed me to contribute to research addressing questions of national and international importance,” stated Osabutey. “As a physician-scientist in training, I could not have asked for a better environment in which to train, and the experience has taught me how to pursue meaningful scientific questions through rigorous basic/translational investigation and collaboration, skills that I will carry forward in my future efforts to better understand brain injury and neurological disease.”.

The research involved a broader collaboration between University of Rochester scientists and personnel at Brookhaven National Laboratory, where particle accelerators generate radiation conditions relevant to spaceflight.

“Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows have been an essential part of our NASA research effort,” O’Banion remarked. “It’s comprised of a large team that includes the outstanding organizational skills of our long-time senior research technician, Lee Trojanczyk, as well as support personnel at Brookhaven National Labs. Over time, nearly a dozen University of Rochester trainees have contributed to this work.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals sex-specific microglial responses to simulated galactic cosmic radiation without broad inflammatory activation” by Mark A. Osabutey, Lia Calcines-Rodríguez, Lee A. Trojanczyk, John A. Olschowka and M. Kerry O’Banion, 20 November 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-77661-9.

This research was supported by a NASA grant and a NASA Human Research Program Grant Augmentation Award.
